docs.title: Sadame
docs.text:
Sadame (定め, "what is ordained") is a configuration management tool: you describe the desired state of a machine in plain Ruby, sadame plan shows the difference as a diff, and sadame apply makes the machine match.

examples/01-hello/recipe.rb
# The smallest useful recipe: one file with fixed content.
file "/tmp/sadame-hello.txt", content: "Hello from sadame!\n"

$ sadame plan examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
    state: absent -> present
    --- /dev/null
    +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
    @@ -0,0 +1 @@
    +Hello from sadame!

Plan: 1 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

Status

Sadame is under development towards 0.1.0. It runs recipes with plan, apply and drift, on the local machine or on remote hosts over SSH with a hosts.rb inventory. The first release is being prepared.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Users run sadame on servers and workstations. Start with Getting started.
  • Recipe authors write recipes for their team. Start with Recipe basics, then the resources.
  • Contributors change sadame itself. Start with Contributing.

docs.title: What does "sadame" mean?
docs.text: 定め (sadame) is Japanese for what has been decided or ordained: here, the state a machine is supposed to be in.

docs.title: Do the servers need Ruby, Python or an agent?
docs.text: No. Sadame is a single static binary. In push mode it copies itself to each target over scp, keyed by checksum, and runs there over ssh; nothing keeps running afterwards. The targets need a POSIX shell, tar, and sha256sum or shasum.

docs.title: Why Ruby for recipes, if the servers do not need Ruby?
docs.text: Recipes are Ruby because a configuration language eventually needs loops, conditions and functions; Ruby has them already, with no YAML templating on top. The binary contains an embedded Ruby (mruby), so recipes run without a Ruby installation anywhere.

docs.title: Can I use gems or Ruby's standard library in recipes?
docs.text: No. The embedded Ruby has no require, no gems and no standard library beyond what sadame includes. JSON.parse, File, ENV and the core classes are available. Most recipe logic needs no more.

docs.title: Which systems are supported?
docs.text: Targets: Debian, Ubuntu, Rocky Linux and other RHEL-like systems, Alpine and Arch Linux (including Omarchy), on x86_64 and ARM64. service needs systemd, so it does not work on Alpine. The machine running sadame can be Linux or macOS. Windows is not supported, as a target or otherwise.

docs.title: How is this different from Ansible?
docs.text: Recipes are Ruby rather than YAML, targets need no Python, plan shows every change as a diff, and drift gives CI a yes-or-no answer. Ansible has far more modules, a large ecosystem, Windows and network device support, and years of production use. See Migrate from Ansible and the comparison table.

docs.title: How is this different from Itamae and mitamae?
docs.text: The recipe language is close to theirs. Sadame adds pushing to remote hosts without installing anything, an inventory, drift, and JSON output; it has fewer resources. See Migrate from Itamae.

docs.title: Is there a pull mode or an agent?
docs.text: No. Sadame runs when you run it, from your machine or CI. For a periodic check, schedule sadame drift; for periodic enforcement, schedule sadame apply.

docs.title: How do I keep secrets out of the repository?
docs.text: Read them from the environment in vars.rb (ENV["DB_PASSWORD"]), which is evaluated on the machine running sadame, and mark files that contain them sensitive: true so their diffs are hidden. There is no built-in encryption like Ansible Vault.

docs.title: Does apply roll back when something fails?
docs.text: No. It stops at the failing resource, leaves what was already changed in place, and reports the rest as skipped. Fix the cause and apply again: only what still differs is changed.

docs.title: Why does my exec show up in every plan?
docs.text: It has no guard, so sadame cannot tell whether its work is done. Add creates:, not_if: or only_if:, or action: :nothing if it should only run when notified.

docs.title: Can sadame upgrade packages?
docs.text: Not in 0.1: package makes sure a package is installed or absent, not that it is the newest version. Upgrade with the package manager, or with a guarded exec.

docs.title: Does sadame support the AUR?
docs.text: Not directly in 0.1. Use an AUR helper through exec; see package.

docs.title: How many hosts can it handle?
docs.text: Every selected host runs at the same time, each in its own process, so the limit is your machine's processes and SSH connections. Sadame has not been tested on fleets of hundreds of hosts; for those, run it in batches with --limit.

docs.title: Where are the logs?
docs.text: Sadame prints to the terminal; with --json it prints a report you can store. It writes no log files on the targets.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes you from a source checkout to your first plan and apply: install sadame, write a one-line recipe, look at the plan, apply it, and learn to read the diff sadame prints when a machine has drifted from its recipe.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install the single binary as described on the Install page, or run sadame from a checkout of the repository with Ruby 3.2 or newer:

git clone https://github.com/enderkus/sadame.git
cd sadame
bin/sadame --version

The rest of this page writes sadame; use bin/sadame if you run it from the checkout.

docs.title: Your first recipe
docs.text:
A recipe is a Ruby file that declares resources: packages, files, directories, services, commands and users. The smallest one has a single resource:

examples/01-hello/recipe.rb
# The smallest useful recipe: one file with fixed content.
file "/tmp/sadame-hello.txt", content: "Hello from sadame!\n"

It writes to /tmp, so it works without root.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
sadame plan reads the current state of everything the recipe declares and prints what apply would change. It changes nothing.

$ sadame plan examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
    state: absent -> present
    --- /dev/null
    +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
    @@ -0,0 +1 @@
    +Hello from sadame!

Plan: 1 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

RECIPE can be a file or a directory that contains recipe.rb. Without it, sadame looks for ./recipe.rb.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
sadame apply makes the same comparison, resource by resource, and changes only what differs:

$ sadame apply examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
           state: absent -> present
           --- /dev/null
           +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
           @@ -0,0 +1 @@
           +Hello from sadame!

Summary
  changed      1  file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
  unchanged    0
  failed       0
  skipped      0
  notified     0

Finished in 0.08s.

Run plan again and there is nothing left to do. That is what idempotent means here: once the machine matches the recipe, running it again changes nothing.

$ sadame plan examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 1 unchanged.

docs.title: Read the diff
docs.text:
Now change the file by hand, the way a colleague or a package upgrade might:

$ echo 'Hello from someone else' > /tmp/sadame-hello.txt

$ sadame plan examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
    --- /tmp/sadame-hello.txt
    +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
    @@ -1 +1 @@
    -Hello from someone else
    +Hello from sadame!

Plan: 0 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

Each resource that would change gets a header line with a symbol and the resource's id, type[name]:

Symbol Meaning + create: the resource does not exist yet ~ update: it exists but some attributes differ - remove: the recipe says state: :absent and it exists ! run: an exec command whose guards say it must run x failed: the current state could not be read; the error follows

Below the header, each differing attribute is shown as current -> desired. File content is shown as a unified diff, the same format as diff -u and git diff: --- is the file on disk, +++ is what the recipe wants. In a terminal, removed lines are red and added lines green:

--- /tmp/sadame-hello.txt
+++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
@@ -1 +1 @@
-Hello from someone else
+Hello from sadame!

Colors are turned off when output is not a terminal, with --no-color, or when the NO_COLOR environment variable is set.

The last line counts resources by what would happen to them. Unchanged resources are counted but not listed.

docs.title: Check for drift
docs.text:
sadame drift reads the same state as plan, but its exit status says whether the machine still matches the recipe: 0 when it does, 1 when it has drifted. That makes it the command for scripts, cron jobs and CI:

$ sadame drift examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev drift on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
    --- /tmp/sadame-hello.txt
    +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
    @@ -1 +1 @@
    -Hello from someone else
    +Hello from sadame!

Drift: 1 of 1 resource differs from the recipe.

$ echo $?
1

Plan, apply, drift explains when to use which, and Drift in CI runs the check on a schedule.

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text: Status plan apply drift 0 the plan was computed, with or without changes every resource and notification succeeded the machine matches the recipe 1 not used a resource or notification failed the machine differs from the recipe 2 usage or recipe error, or the state of a resource could not be read usage or recipe error usage or recipe error, or the state of a resource could not be read

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running without root. Most real recipes install packages or write under /etc. Run them with sudo sadame apply ...; plan usually needs root too, to read files only root can read.
  • Expecting apply to undo things it does not manage. Sadame only compares what the recipe declares. Deleting a resource from a recipe does not remove it from the machine; declare it with state: :absent instead.
  • Treating plan as a guarantee. plan compares each resource with the machine as it is now. During apply, earlier resources change the machine (a package creates a user, a file a service needs), so later resources are compared again right before they run.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Sadame is a single executable with no runtime dependencies: no Ruby, no gems, no libraries. Each release has four builds. The Linux builds are statically linked, so the same file runs on Debian, Ubuntu, Rocky, Alpine, Arch and other distributions.

System CPU File Linux x86_64 sadame-linux-amd64 Linux aarch64 (ARM64) sadame-linux-arm64 macOS 11 or newer Apple silicon sadame-darwin-arm64 macOS 11 or newer Intel sadame-darwin-amd64

Every release also has SHA256SUMS, the SHA-256 checksum of each file.

No release yet

The first release will be 0.1.0. Until it is published, the install script and the download links below return "not found"; install from source instead.

docs.title: Install script
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enderkus/sadame/main/install.sh | sh

The script (install.sh in the repository) picks the file for your system and CPU, downloads it and SHA256SUMS from the latest release, stops if the checksum does not match, and installs the binary as /usr/local/bin/sadame, using sudo if that directory is not writable. It needs curl or wget, and sha256sum or shasum.

Variable Default Effect SADAME_VERSION latest release Install this release, such as v0.1.0. SADAME_INSTALL_DIR /usr/local/bin Install somewhere else, such as $HOME/.local/bin. SADAME_DOWNLOAD_URL the GitHub release Download from a mirror that has the same files. 
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enderkus/sadame/main/install.sh \
  | SADAME_VERSION=v0.1.0 SADAME_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin" sh

Read the script before piping it to a shell if you prefer; it is about 100 lines of POSIX sh.

docs.title: Manual download
docs.text:
Download the binary for your system and SHA256SUMS from the releases page, then check the binary before installing it.

On Linux:

version=v0.1.0
base=https://github.com/enderkus/sadame/releases/download/$version
curl -fsSLO "$base/sadame-linux-amd64"
curl -fsSLO "$base/SHA256SUMS"
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS
sudo install -m 0755 sadame-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/sadame
sadame --version

sha256sum prints sadame-linux-amd64: OK when the file is intact.

On macOS, use shasum:

shasum -a 256 --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS

The macOS binaries are not signed by Apple. Files downloaded with a web browser are quarantined and refused on first run; files downloaded with curl, as above and in the install script, are not. To run a binary you downloaded with a browser, remove the quarantine flag:

xattr -d com.apple.quarantine sadame-darwin-arm64

docs.title: Homebrew
docs.text: Not available yet. A tap is planned, so that brew install enderkus/sadame/sadame installs the macOS and Linux binaries.

docs.title: Arch Linux (AUR)
docs.text: Not available yet. A sadame-bin package that installs the release binary is planned. Until then, use the install script, or exec it from your own recipe.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
Run sadame from a checkout with Ruby 3.2 or newer, no build needed:

git clone https://github.com/enderkus/sadame.git
cd sadame
bin/sadame --version

Or build the binary yourself. rake build:native needs a C compiler, git, bison, Ruby and rake; the static Linux builds need Docker:

rake build:native        # this machine, development build: build/host/bin/sadame
rake build:linux-amd64   # static Linux x86_64: dist/sadame-linux-amd64
rake build:linux-arm64   # static Linux ARM64: dist/sadame-linux-arm64
rake build:macos         # on a Mac: dist/sadame-darwin-arm64 and -amd64

Building sadame explains each target.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
sudo rm /usr/local/bin/sadame

Sadame keeps no other files on the machine it is installed on, except ~/.sadame/dist/, where it keeps binaries it downloaded for pushing to other systems. On machines it was pushed to, it keeps ~/.sadame/ (see Remote hosts).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Picking the wrong CPU. uname -m prints x86_64 for sadame-linux-amd64 and aarch64 (Linux) or arm64 (macOS) for the arm64 builds. The wrong one fails with "Exec format error".
  • Skipping the checksum. A truncated download also fails to run, but a tampered one would not. sha256sum -c takes a second.
  • Installing into a directory not on PATH. With SADAME_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin", make sure that directory is in your PATH.

docs.title: Plan, apply, drift
docs.text:
Sadame has three commands that work on the same comparison: for every resource in the recipe, read the current state from the machine, compare it with the desired state, and report the difference. plan shows the difference, apply removes it, and drift tells you, through its exit status, whether there is any difference left. Used together they form a loop: plan a change, apply it, and later check that the machine has not wandered away from the recipe.

flowchart LR
    recipe["recipe + vars"] --> plan["sadame plan<br/>review the diff"]
    plan --> apply["sadame apply<br/>change what differs"]
    apply --> converged(("machine<br/>matches recipe"))
    converged -->|"later: hand edits,<br/>upgrades, accidents"| drift["sadame drift<br/>in cron or CI"]
    drift -->|"exit 0"| converged
    drift -->|"exit 1: drift found"| plan

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
Command Changes the machine Use it to Exit status plan no review what a recipe or var change would do before applying it 0 whether or not there are changes apply yes converge the machine: change only what differs, then run notifications 0 when everything succeeded, 1 when something failed drift no check, from a script, cron job or CI pipeline, that the machine still matches 0 no difference, 1 difference found

All three exit with 2 when the command line or the recipe is wrong. plan and drift also exit with 2 when they could not read the state of some resource, because they then cannot tell whether it matches:

Status plan apply drift 0 plan computed every resource and notification succeeded machine matches the recipe 1 not used a resource or notification failed machine differs from the recipe 2 usage or recipe error, or a state could not be read usage or recipe error usage or recipe error, or a state could not be read

plan and drift produce the same report; only the summary line and the exit status differ. Both accept --json (see the JSON output reference).

docs.title: The loop on a real machine
docs.text:
The example recipe installs nginx, adds a system user, writes a configuration file and keeps nginx running:

examples/10-drift-demo/recipe.rb
# A small server to watch drift on: a package, a system user, a config file
# and a service. Paths are Debian and Ubuntu's.
package "nginx"

user "demo-app", system: true, home: "/var/lib/demo-app", shell: "/usr/sbin/nologin"

directory "/etc/demo-app", mode: "0755"

file "/etc/demo-app/app.conf",
     template: "app.conf.erb",
     owner: "root",
     group: "demo-app",
     mode: "0640"

service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame apply examples/10-drift-demo
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    package[nginx]
           state: absent -> installed
changed    user[demo-app]
           state: absent -> present
           home: /var/lib/demo-app
           shell: /usr/sbin/nologin
changed    directory[/etc/demo-app]
           state: absent -> present
           mode: 0755
changed    file[/etc/demo-app/app.conf]
           state: absent -> present
           mode: 0640
           owner: root
           group: demo-app
           --- /dev/null
           +++ /etc/demo-app/app.conf (desired)
           @@ -0,0 +1,4 @@
           +# Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
           +listen    = 127.0.0.1:9000
           +workers   = 4
           +log_level = info
changed    service[nginx]
           state: stopped -> running

Summary
  changed      5  package[nginx]
                  user[demo-app]
                  directory[/etc/demo-app]
                  file[/etc/demo-app/app.conf]
                  service[nginx]
  unchanged    0
  failed       0
  skipped      0
  notified     0

Finished in 5.50s.

docs.title: Drift right after apply
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame drift examples/10-drift-demo
sadame 0.1.0.dev drift on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

No drift: 5 resources match the recipe.

$ echo $?
0

docs.title: Something changes the machine
docs.text:
break-things.sh does what happens to servers over time: someone edits a setting by hand, loosens a file's permissions while debugging, and stops a service.

examples/10-drift-demo/break-things.sh
#!/bin/sh
# Simulates what happens to servers over time: a hand edit, a permissions
# "fix" and a stopped service. Run it as root after `sadame apply`, then run
# `sadame drift` to see each change reported.
set -e

# Someone tunes a setting by hand.
sed -i 's/^workers   = .*/workers   = 16/' /etc/demo-app/app.conf

# Someone makes the file world-readable while debugging.
chmod 0644 /etc/demo-app/app.conf

# Someone stops nginx and forgets to start it again.
systemctl stop nginx

echo "break-things: edited app.conf, changed its mode, stopped nginx"

$ sudo sh examples/10-drift-demo/break-things.sh
break-things: edited app.conf, changed its mode, stopped nginx

docs.title: Drift catches it
docs.text:
Three changes on two resources: the file's content and mode, and the service state. The exit status is 1.

$ sudo sadame drift examples/10-drift-demo
sadame 0.1.0.dev drift on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ file[/etc/demo-app/app.conf]
    mode: 0644 -> 0640
    --- /etc/demo-app/app.conf
    +++ /etc/demo-app/app.conf (desired)
    @@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
     # Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
     listen    = 127.0.0.1:9000
    -workers   = 16
    +workers   = 4
     log_level = info

~ service[nginx]
    state: stopped -> running

Drift: 2 of 5 resources differ from the recipe.

$ echo $?
1

docs.title: Apply puts it back
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame apply examples/10-drift-demo
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

unchanged  package[nginx]
unchanged  user[demo-app]
unchanged  directory[/etc/demo-app]
changed    file[/etc/demo-app/app.conf]
           mode: 0644 -> 0640
           --- /etc/demo-app/app.conf
           +++ /etc/demo-app/app.conf (desired)
           @@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
            # Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
            listen    = 127.0.0.1:9000
           -workers   = 16
           +workers   = 4
            log_level = info
changed    service[nginx]
           state: stopped -> running

Summary
  changed      2  file[/etc/demo-app/app.conf]
                  service[nginx]
  unchanged    3
  failed       0
  skipped      0
  notified     0

Finished in 0.01s.

$ sudo sadame drift examples/10-drift-demo
sadame 0.1.0.dev drift on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

No drift: 5 resources match the recipe.

$ echo $?
0

docs.title: What drift sees, and what it does not
docs.text:
Drift compares only what the recipe declares, attribute by attribute:

  • A file's content, mode, owner and group, but only those you set. A file declared without mode: can change mode without drift.
  • Packages, by name: an installed package of any version matches state: :installed.
  • Services: only enable: and state:, when given.
  • exec resources: the guard decides. An exec whose guard says it must run counts as drift, and an exec without any guard always does.
  • Anything not in the recipe is invisible: files nobody declared, extra packages, extra users.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unguarded exec resources. They make drift exit 1 forever. Give every exec a guard, or action: :nothing if it only runs when notified.
  • Running drift without root. Files only root can read cannot be compared; those resources fail and drift exits 2, not 1.
  • Treating plan's exit status as drift. plan exits 0 even when there are changes. Scripts that need a yes/no answer use drift.
  • Expecting drift to repair. drift never changes anything. Run apply to converge, after reviewing the diff.

docs.title: Contributing to Sadame
docs.text: Thank you for helping. This guide covers setting up a development checkout, running the tests on both Ruby runtimes, the rules that keep the code working under mruby, and what a pull request needs.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
You need:

  • Ruby 3.2 or newer and Bundler, for running sadame from source and for the test suite;
  • a C compiler, git and bison, for building the mruby binary.
git clone https://github.com/enderkus/sadame.git
cd sadame
bundle install

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The same test files run under CRuby (with minitest) and inside the mruby build (with mruby-mtest). CI requires both to pass.

bundle exec rake test:cruby   # fast, no compiler needed
bundle exec rake test:mruby   # builds mruby with sadame into build/, then runs the suite
bundle exec rake test         # both

rake build:native builds a development binary into build/host/bin/sadame. Release binaries, static Linux builds through Docker and the macOS builds, are described in Building sadame.

Tests never need root: resources are tested against FakeShell (test/support/fake_shell.rb), which records commands and returns stubbed results.

docs.title: Writing code for mruby
docs.text:
Release builds are a single mruby binary, so everything under lib/ must run on mruby with only the gems listed in build_config.rb:

  • Never call require in lib/. To add a file, list it with require_relative in lib/sadame.rb; the mruby build reads that list to compile the same files in the same order.
  • No standard library (JSON, YAML, ERB, Open3, FileUtils, ...). Sadame has small replacements: Sadame::JsonWriter, Sadame::Template, Sadame::Shell.escape.
  • Run commands and read files only through Sadame::Shell.
  • In a rescue clause, re-raise with raise e, not a bare raise.

The full list of pitfalls, with what to use instead, is in Architecture. If you think a new mruby gem is needed, explain why in the commit that adds it to build_config.rb.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• Clear names, small methods, plain classes. No metaprogramming beyond what the recipe DSL needs.
  • Every resource reads the current state before acting and does nothing when it matches the desired state.
  • Errors meant for users are Sadame::Error subclasses with a message that says what to do.

docs.title: Documentation and examples
docs.text:
Documentation is part of every change:

  • A new feature comes with a page (or a section) in docs/ following the feature page shape: what and why, a minimal example, an option table, realistic scenarios with real output, common mistakes, see also.
  • Every recipe shown in the docs lives under examples/ and is embedded with --8<-- "examples/...". test/unit/examples_test.rb loads, plans and applies every example against a fake machine and checks that every examples/ path mentioned in the docs exists.
  • Terminal sessions in the docs are captured, not typed. Each one is defined in script/transcripts/scenarios.rb, run in a fresh Docker container by rake docs:transcripts (or SCENARIO=name rake docs:transcripts for one), written to docs/transcripts/, and embedded with --8<-- "docs/transcripts/NAME.txt". Short excerpts, such as a diff shown on its own, are copied from those files. When a change alters output, regenerate the transcripts and commit them with the change.

Build the site locally with:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Sadame is a small Ruby program that has to run in two places: on CRuby during development and tests, and compiled into a single mruby binary for users. This page maps the code, follows one run through it, lists the rules that keep the code working on mruby, and walks through the two most common extensions: a new resource and a new package manager.

docs.title: Module map
docs.text:
All code lives in lib/sadame/. lib/sadame.rb lists the files in load order; the mruby build compiles the same list.

File Responsibility cli.rb Parses arguments, loads vars, the inventory and the recipe, runs a command locally or through push mode, returns the exit status. Sadame.main is the entry point of the binary. inventory.rb The hosts.rb language, groups and includes, and selecting targets with -h, -g and --limit, including each target's merged vars. target.rb A host to push to, and parsing [user@]host[:port]. glob.rb * and ? matching for --limit. hosts_listing.rb The output of sadame hosts. push/run.rb Push mode: bundles the recipe, detects each target's system, finds binaries, runs every target, prints the summary or the combined JSON. push/session.rb One target: copies the binary (once per checksum) and the recipe, runs sadame there. push/ssh.rb The ssh and scp command lines for a target. push/binary_store.rb Finds the binary for a target's system on the machine running sadame, downloading and checking it if needed. push/parallel.rb Runs one child process per target and prints their output as it arrives. ruby_literal.rb Writes values as Ruby source, to send vars to targets and results between processes. vars.rb Loads vars.rb, parses --var, merges layers. recipe.rb The recipe DSL: package, file, ..., include_recipe, vars, platform. Evaluates recipe files with instance_eval. resource_collection.rb The ordered resources of a run, duplicate detection, and the notification index. resource.rb Base class: option validation, desired / current / diff / apply, notification actions. resources/*.rb One class per resource type. notification.rb Parses notifies: and subscribes: entries. runner.rb Runs plan, drift and apply over a collection; queues and runs notifications. report.rb The result of a run: entries, notification runs, counts, exit status, JSON shape. output.rb Renders a report as text (as it happens) or as JSON (at the end). diff.rb Attribute changes and unified diffs (Myers' algorithm). template.rb The ERB-compatible template engine. host.rb The machine being configured: its shell plus facts read once (platform, package manager, systemd). platform.rb Reads /etc/os-release; maps distributions to families and package managers. package_managers/*.rb apt, dnf, apk and pacman: the command lines for query, install and remove. path_stat.rb Type, mode, owner and group of a path, from stat. shell.rb The only place commands run and files are read or written. json_writer.rb JSON generation, identical on both runtimes. errors.rb Error classes and recipe error locations.

docs.title: One run, step by step
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    cli["CLI: parse arguments"] --> vars["Vars: vars.rb + --var"]
    vars --> recipe["Recipe.load: evaluate recipe files"]
    recipe --> collection["ResourceCollection<br/>+ linked notifications"]
    collection --> runner["Runner: plan / drift / apply"]
    runner --> resource["Resource#diff<br/>desired vs current"]
    resource --> shell["Shell: commands, files"]
    runner --> report["Report"]
    report --> output["Output: text or JSON"]
    report --> status["exit status"]
  1. CLI parses the arguments and finds the recipe and vars.rb.
  2. Recipe.load evaluates the recipe in a Recipe object. Each DSL call builds a resource, which validates its options right away, and adds it to the ResourceCollection. After the last file, the collection links notifications and checks that every target exists.
  3. Runner walks the collection. For each resource it calls diff, which compares desired with current. current reads the machine through the Shell of the Host; nothing else touches the system.
  4. For apply, a non-empty diff is passed to the resource's apply, and the notifications it triggers run immediately or are queued.
  5. Each result goes to a Report and to the Output, which prints text as the run progresses or JSON at the end. Report#exit_status becomes the process exit status.

In push mode, steps 2 to 5 happen on each target: CLI loads the inventory, Inventory#select turns the flags into Targets with their vars, and Push::Run copies the binary and the recipe to each target and runs sadame COMMAND there with --vars-file, --host-name and --host-groups, in one child process per target. The targets' own reports are streamed back (text) or collected into one document (JSON).

docs.title: Code that must run on mruby
docs.text:
Release builds are mruby, so code in lib/ may only use the language and the gems in build_config.rb. CI runs the whole test suite on both runtimes, which catches most mistakes, but these are the ones that come up:

Do not use Because Use instead require, require_relative in lib/ mruby has no loader; the build compiles a fixed file list add the file to lib/sadame.rb JSON, YAML, ERB, Open3, FileUtils, Shellwords, OptionParser, Set, Net::* no standard library JsonWriter, Template, Shell, Shell.escape, plain loops Integer#zero?, #even?, #odd?, #positive? not in the included gems == 0, % 2 enumerators without a block: each_slice(2).to_a, map.with_index, each_char.map mruby's enumerators need fibers, which are not built in blocks, each_with_index with a block, chars catch / throw not built in return values File.basename(path, ".rb") only one argument is supported File.basename(path).delete_suffix(".rb") bare raise in a rescue clause mruby 3.4 raises a new RuntimeError rescue Foo => e and raise e backticks, system, Process.spawn they bypass Shell, and spawn does not exist Shell#run, Shell#run! inspect output in user-facing messages its format differs between runtimes format values explicitly instance_eval with a string at the top level of a script mruby then defines later top-level methods on the wrong object call it inside a method

Strings are byte strings in the mruby build ("é".size is 2), which only matters when counting characters for alignment.

docs.title: Adding a resource
docs.text: This section builds a cron resource that manages one job as a file in /etc/cron.d. Sadame does not ship it; the code below is kept in test/unit/tutorial_cron_test.rb, where it is compiled and tested on both runtimes like the real resources.

docs.title: 1. Decide what the desired state is
docs.text: A resource is a set of attributes whose current value can be read and compared. For a cron job that is whether the file exists (state) and its exact text (content). Using the attribute name content means plan output and JSON show changes as a unified diff, like the file resource does.

docs.title: 2. Write the class
docs.text:
In a real change this goes into lib/sadame/resources/cron.rb:

  # Manages one cron job as a file in /etc/cron.d.
  #
  #   cron "backup", schedule: "0 3 * * *", command: "/usr/local/bin/backup"
  class CronResource < Sadame::Resource
    STATES = %w[present absent].freeze
    NAME_CHARACTERS = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789-_"

    def self.type_name
      "cron"
    end

    def self.allowed_options
      [:schedule, :command, :user, :state]
    end

    def path
      "/etc/cron.d/#{name}"
    end

    def desired
      return { state: "absent" } if absent?

      { state: "present", content: "#{options[:schedule]} #{user} #{options[:command]}\n" }
    end

    def current
      content = shell.read_file(path)
      return { state: "absent" } if content.nil?

      { state: "present", content: content }
    end

    def apply(_changes)
      if absent?
        shell.run!("rm -f #{quote(path)}")
      else
        shell.write_file(path, desired[:content])
        shell.run!("chmod 0644 #{quote(path)}")
      end
    end

    private

    def validate
      validate_choice(:state, STATES)
      unless name.chars.all? { |char| NAME_CHARACTERS.include?(char) }
        raise Sadame::ResourceError, "#{id}: cron.d file names may only use letters, digits, - and _"
      end
      return if absent?

      [:schedule, :command].each do |key|
        raise Sadame::ResourceError, "#{id}: #{key} is required" unless options[key].is_a?(String)
      end
      return if options[:schedule].split(" ").size == 5

      raise Sadame::ResourceError, "#{id}: schedule needs five fields, such as \"0 3 * * *\""
    end

    def absent?
      options[:state].to_s == "absent"
    end

    def user
      options[:user] || "root"
    end
  end

What the base class does for you:

  • allowed_options is checked when the recipe loads: an unknown option fails before anything runs. notifies: and subscribes: are always allowed.
  • validate runs right after, for option values.
  • diff compares desired with current, attribute by attribute. Only keys present in desired are compared.
  • plan_action turns a state change from "absent" into a create and a change to "absent" into a remove.
  • apply is only called with a non-empty diff.

Two rules to keep: read the machine only through shell (never File directly), and make apply change only what differs.

docs.title: 3. Register it
docs.text:
Add the file to lib/sadame.rb, after resource_collection and before recipe:

require_relative "sadame/resources/cron"

and add the DSL method to Sadame::Recipe in lib/sadame/recipe.rb. The tutorial does it in a subclass to leave the real DSL alone:

  # In lib/sadame/recipe.rb this is one more method of Sadame::Recipe; the
  # tutorial adds it in a subclass to keep the real DSL unchanged.
  class Recipe < Sadame::Recipe
    def cron(name, options = {})
      declare(CronResource, name, options)
    end
  end

A recipe can now declare cron jobs:

test/fixtures/recipes/tutorial_cron/recipe.rb
cron "backup", schedule: "0 3 * * *", command: "/usr/local/bin/backup"
cron "cleanup", schedule: "*/15 * * * *", command: "find /tmp/app -mtime +1 -delete", user: "app"

docs.title: 4. Test it without root
docs.text:
Tests run against FakeShell, which records commands and keeps files in memory, so they need no root and touch nothing. Cover creating, the no-change case, an update, removal and validation:

  def cron(options, shell)
    build_resource(Tutorial::CronResource, "backup", options, shell: shell)
  end

  def test_creates_a_missing_job
    shell = linux_shell
    job = cron({ schedule: "0 3 * * *", command: "/usr/local/bin/backup" }, shell)
    changes = job.diff
    assert_equal :create, job.plan_action(changes)

    job.apply(changes)
    assert_equal "0 3 * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup\n", shell.files["/etc/cron.d/backup"]
    assert_equal "chmod 0644 /etc/cron.d/backup", shell.commands.last
  end

  def test_matching_job_has_no_changes
    shell = linux_shell
    shell.files["/etc/cron.d/backup"] = "0 3 * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup\n"
    assert_empty cron({ schedule: "0 3 * * *", command: "/usr/local/bin/backup" }, shell).diff
  end

  def test_changed_schedule_is_an_update
    shell = linux_shell
    shell.files["/etc/cron.d/backup"] = "0 3 * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup\n"
    job = cron({ schedule: "30 4 * * *", command: "/usr/local/bin/backup" }, shell)
    changes = job.diff
    assert_equal :update, job.plan_action(changes)
    assert_equal [:content], change_attributes(changes)
  end

  def test_removes_a_job
    shell = linux_shell
    shell.files["/etc/cron.d/backup"] = "0 3 * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup\n"
    job = cron({ state: :absent }, shell)
    job.apply(job.diff)
    assert_equal "rm -f /etc/cron.d/backup", shell.commands.last
  end

  def test_validation
    error = assert_raises(Sadame::ResourceError) { cron({ schedule: "daily", command: "x" }, linux_shell) }
    assert_includes error.message, "schedule needs five fields"
    error = assert_raises(Sadame::ResourceError) { cron({ schedule: "0 3 * * *" }, linux_shell) }
    assert_includes error.message, "command is required"
  end

Run bundle exec rake test to check both runtimes.

docs.title: 5. Document it
docs.text:
1. Write docs/resources/cron.md in the feature page shape: what and why, minimal example, option table, scenarios, common mistakes, see also.
  2. Put every recipe the page shows in a new cron directory under examples/resources/ and add them to EXAMPLES in test/unit/examples_test.rb.
  3. Add a scenario to script/transcripts/scenarios.rb that runs the examples, run SCENARIO=cron rake docs:transcripts, and embed the transcripts.
  4. Add the page to mkdocs.yml and an entry to CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Adding a package manager
docs.text: This section adds zypper, for openSUSE. Like the cron resource, the code is kept in test/unit/tutorial_zypper_test.rb.

docs.title: 1. Write the class
docs.text:
A package manager only provides three command lines; Base runs them and turns exit statuses into results. In a real change this goes into lib/sadame/package_managers/zypper.rb:

  # openSUSE and SUSE Linux Enterprise.
  class Zypper < Sadame::PackageManagers::Base
    def name
      "zypper"
    end

    def query_command(package)
      "rpm -q #{Sadame::Shell.escape(package)}"
    end

    def install_command(package, options = nil)
      "zypper --non-interactive install #{extra_flags(options)}#{Sadame::Shell.escape(package)}"
    end

    def remove_command(package, options = nil)
      "zypper --non-interactive remove #{extra_flags(options)}#{Sadame::Shell.escape(package)}"
    end
  end

Override installed? when the query's exit status is not enough, as Apt does with dpkg-query, and install when the index needs refreshing, as Apt does with apt-get update.

docs.title: 2. Register it
docs.text:
• Add require_relative "sadame/package_managers/zypper" to lib/sadame.rb, before sadame/package_managers.
  • Add "zypper" => Zypper to PackageManagers::ALL in lib/sadame/package_managers.rb.
  • Teach Platform the family: add "suse" => %w[opensuse-leap opensuse-tumbleweed sles] to FAMILY_IDS and "suse" => "zypper" to PACKAGE_MANAGERS in lib/sadame/platform.rb.

docs.title: 3. Test it
docs.text:
Add the distribution's real /etc/os-release as a fixture under test/fixtures/os-release/ (copy it from the official container image) and a platform test for it. Then test the exact command lines:

  def test_zypper_command_lines
    zypper = Tutorial::Zypper.new(linux_shell)
    assert_equal "rpm -q nginx", zypper.query_command("nginx")
    assert_equal "zypper --non-interactive install nginx", zypper.install_command("nginx")
    assert_equal "zypper --non-interactive remove nginx", zypper.remove_command("nginx")
    assert_equal "zypper --non-interactive install --no-recommends nginx",
                 zypper.install_command("nginx", "--no-recommends")
  end

  def test_zypper_installs_through_the_shell
    shell = linux_shell.on("rpm -q nginx", exit_status: 1)
    zypper = Tutorial::Zypper.new(shell)
    refute zypper.installed?("nginx")
    zypper.install("nginx")
    assert_equal "zypper --non-interactive install nginx", shell.commands.last
  end

docs.title: 4. Document it
docs.text: Add a row to the command table in docs/resources/package.md, capture a transcript on that distribution, and update CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading files with File in a resource. It works on CRuby and in production, but tests then read your machine instead of FakeShell. Use shell.read_file.
  • Forgetting lib/sadame.rb. Neither runtime loads a file that is not listed there: CRuby follows its require_relative lines and the mruby build compiles exactly those files.
  • Changing output without regenerating transcripts. Run rake docs:transcripts and commit the changed files in docs/transcripts/.

docs.title: Building sadame
docs.text: Sadame's Ruby code in lib/ is compiled together with mruby into one executable. This page explains the build targets, what each produces, how the release binaries are checked before they are published, and how to fix common build problems.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Task Runs on Produces Used for rake build:native any Unix build/host/bin/sadame and build/host/bin/mruby development; rake test:mruby rake build:linux-amd64 any machine with Docker dist/sadame-linux-amd64 releases rake build:linux-arm64 any machine with Docker dist/sadame-linux-arm64 releases rake build:macos macOS with Xcode command line tools dist/sadame-darwin-arm64, dist/sadame-darwin-amd64 releases rake verify:linux-amd64, verify:linux-arm64 Docker runs the binary in several distributions releases rake verify:macos macOS runs both macOS binaries releases rake checksums any dist/SHA256SUMS releases

The first build clones mruby 3.4.0 into vendor/ and the third-party gems into build/*/repos/. Both directories are ignored by git.

docs.title: How the build is put together
docs.text:
• build_config.rb is mruby's build configuration. sadame_gems lists every mruby gem in the binary; adding one needs a reason in the commit message. The SADAME_TARGET environment variable selects one of four configurations: development (debug information, plus an mruby interpreter with mruby-mtest for the tests), linux-static, darwin-arm64 and darwin-amd64. The Rakefile sets it.
  • build_config.rb.lock pins each third-party gem to a commit. mruby writes it on the first build and reads it afterwards, so every build uses the same code. Commit it when it changes.
  • mrbgem.rake turns sadame into an mruby gem. It reads the require_relative lines of lib/sadame.rb and compiles those files in that order, so CRuby and mruby load the same code the same way.
  • tools/sadame/sadame.c is the main function: it builds ARGV, calls Sadame.main and turns the returned Integer into the exit status.

docs.title: Static Linux binaries
docs.text:
rake build:linux-amd64 and rake build:linux-arm64 build inside an Alpine Linux container of the target architecture (script/build/alpine.Dockerfile). Alpine uses musl libc, which links statically without the problems glibc has with static binaries, so the result runs on any Linux distribution of that architecture. The container runs as your user, so the files in build/ and dist/ stay yours, and the binary is stripped with the container's strip.

Building for the other architecture than your machine's needs an emulator registered with Docker. Docker Desktop and OrbStack include one; on a Linux machine, register QEMU once:

docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install arm64

Emulated builds are slower, especially under QEMU.

docs.title: macOS binaries
docs.text: rake build:macos compiles both macOS binaries on one Mac with clang's -arch flag, targeting macOS 11 and newer. It uses mruby's cross-build support, so the mrbc compiler used during the build runs natively.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Before a binary is published, it has to run unmodified in the systems it is meant for. rake verify:linux-amd64 and rake verify:linux-arm64 start each of these images with the binary mounted, and run script/build/smoke-test.sh inside it:

Image amd64 arm64 ubuntu:24.04 yes yes debian:12 yes yes rockylinux/rockylinux:9 yes yes alpine:3.20 yes yes archlinux:latest yes no arm64 image exists menci/archlinuxarm:latest no yes (community image of Arch Linux ARM)

The smoke test runs --version, then plan, apply and drift on examples/01-hello, edits the managed file, and checks that drift now exits 1 and reports "drift": true in JSON. rake verify:macos runs the same test with both macOS binaries; the Intel one runs through Rosetta when it is installed.

docs.title: Continuous integration and releases
docs.text:
• .github/workflows/build.yml builds linux-amd64 on an x86_64 runner, linux-arm64 on an ARM64 runner and both macOS binaries on a macOS runner. A separate job then registers QEMU with tonistiigi/binfmt, checks with file that both Linux binaries are statically linked, and runs the verification for both architectures on the x86_64 runner: the arm64 binary runs under emulation there. A last job serves the binaries over HTTP and runs install.sh against them, once with correct checksums and once with a wrong one, which must fail.
  • ci.yml runs that workflow on every push and pull request, after the test jobs.
  • release.yml runs on a v* tag. After the build workflow passes, it checks that the tag matches Sadame::VERSION, writes SHA256SUMS, takes the release notes from the matching section of CHANGELOG.md, and creates the GitHub release with all files attached. Started by hand from the Actions tab, it does everything except publishing and keeps the assembled files as a workflow artifact instead.

To publish a release:

  1. Set VERSION in lib/sadame/version.rb and move the Unreleased entries of CHANGELOG.md under a heading such as ## [0.1.0] - 2026-11-15.
  2. Commit, then tag and push: git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0.

docs.title: Building a release locally
docs.text:
rake build:linux-amd64 build:linux-arm64 verify:linux-amd64 verify:linux-arm64
rake build:macos verify:macos      # on a Mac
rake checksums
script/build/test-install.sh       # install.sh against dist/

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
• exec format error while building the other architecture. No emulator is registered; run the tonistiigi/binfmt command above.
  • A gem fails to clone. Builds need network access to GitHub on the first run. After that the gems in build/*/repos/ are reused.
  • The lock file changed unexpectedly. A new build target or a new gem adds entries to build_config.rb.lock. Check the diff and commit it.
  • Stale objects after changing build_config.rb. Delete the target's directory under build/ and build again.

docs.text:

  • Install for the user side of the release files.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Sadame is tested in three layers. Each catches what the one before cannot: the unit tests check sadame's own logic quickly and without root; the Docker tests run every example for real on five distributions and two CPU architectures; the VM tests run them on real machines that boot like servers do. For every layer and every distribution an example applies to, the rule is the same: sadame apply succeeds, and sadame drift right after it exits 0.

Layer Where Runs Needs Unit test/unit/ every commit, in CI, on CRuby 3.2 to 3.4 and inside the mruby build Ruby; a C compiler for mruby Docker test/integration/docker/, test/integration/push/ every push and pull request, in CI, on amd64 and arm64 Docker; the static binaries VM test/integration/vm/ by hand, on the maintainer's machines, never in CI libvirt VMs and hosts.local.rb

docs.title: Which example runs where
docs.text: test/support/example_matrix.rb lists every example, the distributions it supports and why it skips the others. The unit tests and the Docker tests both read it, so they cannot disagree. Some examples only count as passing after the VM layer, because they need a real kernel and boot to be trusted: 03-nginx-tls-certbot (certificates, a public endpoint), 07-hardening-baseline (firewall and sshd) and 12-omarchy-workstation (user sessions; it only runs fully on the Omarchy VM). Their READMEs say so.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
bundle exec rake test:cruby   # minitest on CRuby
bundle exec rake test:mruby   # the same files with mruby-mtest, inside the mruby build
bundle exec rake test         # both

Resources are tested against FakeShell (test/support/fake_shell.rb), which records the commands a resource runs and returns stubbed results, so the tests need no root and change nothing. FreshHostShell stands in for a machine where nothing is configured yet. Among the unit tests:

  • every resource, including the exact command lines of each package manager (pacman's included);
  • every example, planned and applied on a fake machine of every distribution the matrix lists for it, and every inventory under examples/ (the cloud ones against recorded CLI output);
  • the tutorials' code in docs/contributing/architecture.md;
  • that every examples/ path the docs mention exists.

docs.title: Docker integration tests
docs.text:
rake build:linux-amd64 build:linux-arm64       # the binaries under test
rake "test:docker[debian,amd64]"               # one distribution and architecture
rake "test:docker[all,arm64]"                  # every distribution, arm64
rake test:docker                               # every distribution, this machine's architecture
rake test:push                                 # push mode over SSH

rake test:docker starts one fresh container per example, from images in test/integration/docker/images/ built with docker buildx: Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 12, Rocky Linux 9, Alpine 3.20 and Arch Linux (archlinux:latest on amd64; the community image menci/archlinuxarm on arm64, where Arch has no official image). The containers boot systemd as PID 1 (privileged, with the host's cgroups), so service resources start and stop real units. Alpine uses OpenRC, not systemd, so the examples with service resources are skipped there, with that reason in the report. The binary under test is dist/sadame-linux-ARCH, mounted unmodified.

For each example the test runs its setup (for example creating the user that example 12 manages), then for each argument list in the matrix: sadame apply must exit 0 and sadame drift must exit 0. 10-drift-demo also runs break-things.sh and expects drift to exit 1, then applies again. 03-nginx-tls-certbot gets a second container running Pebble, Let's Encrypt's test server, which accepts every challenge, so certbot really requests and installs a certificate without a public domain.

The report lists every example as pass, fail or skip, with the reason for each skip and the last lines of output for each failure.

rake test:push is the push-mode part of this layer. It starts SSH servers that boot systemd: three targets named like examples/08-multi-role-inventory's hosts, db1.example.com with sshd on port 2222, a bastion, and a host on a network only the bastion reaches. A controller container with nothing but the OpenSSH client then checks, among other things, -h user@host:2222, port: 2222 in hosts.rb, a ProxyJump host from a test-scoped SSH configuration passed with -F, vars precedence on the targets, sudo, a parallel run of example 08 on all three hosts, and an unreachable host.

docs.title: What arm64 coverage means
docs.text:
In CI, arm64 runs on x86_64 machines under QEMU, registered with tonistiigi/binfmt: the arm64 binary and the arm64 distribution images, emulated instruction by instruction. That tests the arm64 build and the arm64 packages of each distribution, but not real arm64 hardware; there is no arm64 VM in the VM layer yet. On an ARM64 machine (such as a Mac with Apple silicon running Docker), rake test:docker runs arm64 natively.

Emulation has limits. QEMU's user mode cannot run iptables or nftables, so 04-docker-host (Docker's daemon) and 07-hardening-baseline (ufw) are skipped where the containers are emulated, with that reason in the report; they run in the amd64 jobs and natively on ARM64 machines. Under Rosetta (Docker Desktop and OrbStack on Apple silicon), an x86_64 Arch Linux container could not boot its systemd (version 262) in our tests, so run the amd64 tests in CI or on an x86_64 machine.

docs.title: Running the Docker tests in CI
docs.text: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs rake "test:docker[DISTRO,ARCH]" for all ten combinations, plus rake test:push, after the build workflow has made and verified the binaries. Each combination is its own job, so one failing distribution does not hide the others.

docs.title: VM tests
docs.text:
The VM layer runs the examples on libvirt virtual machines that the maintainer keeps at home, one per distribution: Ubuntu, Debian, Rocky, Arch and Omarchy. It is never wired to CI: the machines and how to reach them are private, so the details live in test/integration/vm/hosts.local.rb, which git ignores. hosts.example.rb next to it shows the shape: one group per distribution with the VM's address, user, port, sudo, and vars naming its libvirt domain and clean snapshot, plus a hypervisor group for the machine running libvirt.

cp test/integration/vm/hosts.example.rb test/integration/vm/hosts.local.rb   # then edit it
rake build:linux-amd64
rake "vm:reset[debian]"     # revert the debian VM to its clean snapshot (virsh over SSH)
rake "vm:test[debian]"      # reset, push every example that applies, check drift after each
rake vm:test:all            # every VM in hosts.local.rb

vm:test reverts the VM, then pushes each applicable example to it from the machine running the tests, through the inventory, and checks that drift exits 0. 07-hardening-baseline runs last, because it moves SSH to port 2222, and its drift check connects to the new port. For example 03, Pebble is started on the VM first. On the Omarchy VM only examples 01 and 12 run; example 12 runs on no other VM. Without hosts.local.rb, the vm: tasks print what is missing and exit 0.

  • Testing amd64 Arch on a Mac. See the emulation note above; use CI.

docs.title: Drift in CI
docs.text: Servers drift: someone edits a file by hand during an incident, a package upgrade rewrites a configuration, a service gets stopped and stays stopped. This guide sets up a scheduled CI job that runs sadame drift --json against every server in the inventory, fails the pipeline when one no longer matches its recipe, and keeps the JSON report as an artifact, so the failure tells you exactly what changed and where. Examples are given for GitHub Actions and GitLab CI.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The CI job installs sadame, loads an SSH key from the CI secrets, and runs:

sadame drift site/site.rb -g all --json > drift.json

Sadame connects to every host of the all group, copies itself there the first time, compares each host with the recipe without changing anything, and writes one JSON document with every host's report (see Remote hosts). Its exit status decides the job:

Exit status Meaning Pipeline 0 every server matches the recipe passes 1 at least one server differs from the recipe fails 2 a server could not be checked: unreachable, a recipe error, or a state sadame could not read fails

On the console, the same run shows each host's differences prefixed with its name, and a summary:

$ sadame drift site.rb --limit 'web*'
[web1.example.com] sadame 0.1.0.dev drift on web1.example.com (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))
[web1.example.com]
[web2.example.com] sadame 0.1.0.dev drift on web2.example.com (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))
[web2.example.com]
[web2.example.com] ~ file[/etc/demo-app/web.conf]
[web2.example.com]     --- /etc/demo-app/web.conf
[web2.example.com]     +++ /etc/demo-app/web.conf (desired)
[web2.example.com]     @@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
[web2.example.com]      # Managed by sadame.
[web2.example.com]      environment = production
[web2.example.com]     -workers     = 12
[web2.example.com]     +workers     = 8
[web2.example.com]
[web2.example.com] Drift: 1 of 6 resources differs from the recipe.
[web1.example.com] No drift: 6 resources match the recipe.

Hosts
  web1.example.com  ok
  web2.example.com  drift

drift on 2 hosts: 1 ok, 1 drift. Finished in 0.22s.

$ echo $?
1

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The recipe and its hosts.rb in the repository, here in site/.
  • A key pair for CI. Its public half goes in authorized_keys of the users named in hosts.rb; its private half is the SSH_PRIVATE_KEY secret.
  • SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS: the output of ssh-keyscan for every server, so the job verifies host keys instead of trusting whatever answers.
  • Passwordless sudo for those users, when the recipe needs root (most do; drift reads files only root can read).

The CI job installs sadame with install.sh, which downloads the latest release. Until the first release (0.1.0) is published, there is nothing to download; build sadame from source in the job instead (see Install).

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Copy this to .github/workflows/drift.yml and add the two secrets under Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions:

examples/ci/github-actions-drift.yml
# Checks the servers in the inventory for drift every morning and fails the
# workflow when one differs from the recipe. The JSON report is kept as an
# artifact either way.
#
# Copy to .github/workflows/drift.yml in the repository that holds your
# recipe (here in site/, with site/hosts.rb). It needs repository secrets
# SSH_PRIVATE_KEY (a key the hosts.rb users accept) and SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS (the
# output of `ssh-keyscan` for every server), and passwordless sudo on the
# servers if the recipe needs root.
name: Drift

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  drift:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install sadame
        run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enderkus/sadame/main/install.sh | sh

      - name: Set up SSH
        run: |
          install -d -m 0700 ~/.ssh
          printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
          chmod 0600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
          printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS }}" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts

      # Exit status: 0 no drift, 1 drift on a server, 2 a server could not be
      # checked. Anything but 0 fails this step and the workflow.
      - name: Check for drift
        run: sadame drift site/site.rb -g all --json > drift.json

      - name: Keep the drift report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: drift-report
          path: drift.json

if: always() on the upload step is what keeps the report when the drift step fails, which is when you need it. The report appears under the run's Artifacts as drift-report.

docs.title: GitLab CI
docs.text:
Add this job to .gitlab-ci.yml, add the two values as CI/CD variables, and create a pipeline schedule under Build > Pipeline schedules:

examples/ci/gitlab-ci-drift.yml
# Checks the servers in the inventory for drift in scheduled pipelines and
# fails the job when one differs from the recipe. The JSON report is kept as
# an artifact either way.
#
# Add this job to .gitlab-ci.yml in the project that holds your recipe (here
# in site/, with site/hosts.rb) and create a pipeline schedule. It needs
# CI/CD variables SSH_PRIVATE_KEY and SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS (masked, protected),
# and passwordless sudo on the servers if the recipe needs root.
drift:
  image: alpine:3.20
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "web"
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache openssh-client
    - wget -qO- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enderkus/sadame/main/install.sh | sh
    - install -d -m 0700 ~/.ssh
    - printf '%s\n' "$SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    - chmod 0600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    - printf '%s\n' "$SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts
  script:
    # Exit status: 0 no drift, 1 drift on a server, 2 a server could not be checked.
    - sadame drift site/site.rb -g all --json > drift.json
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - drift.json
    expire_in: 30 days

artifacts: when: always keeps drift.json on failed jobs too.

docs.title: Reading the report
docs.text:
The report has one entry per host with its status and full report; the format is in the JSON output reference. This lists the resources that drifted, per host:

jq -r '.hosts[] | .name as $host | (.report.resources // [])[]
       | select(.status != "unchanged") | "\($host): \(.id) \(.status)"' drift.json

and this the hosts that could not be checked:

jq -r '.hosts[] | select(.status == "error" or .status == "unreachable") | "\(.name): \(.error)"' drift.json

Sadame's own CI runs sadame drift --json on its runner on every push, edits a managed file, and expects exit status 1; see .github/workflows/ci.yml in the repository.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unguarded exec resources. They count as drift on every run, so the job never passes. Give each one a guard or action: :nothing.
  • No sudo. Without it, files only root can read fail to compare and the job exits 2 instead of telling you about drift.
  • Losing the report on failure. Without if: always() (GitHub) or when: always (GitLab), the upload step is skipped exactly when drift is found.
  • Trusting any host key. StrictHostKeyChecking=no lets anyone who can answer for a server's name read your recipe and its vars. Pin the keys with SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS.
  • Applying from the drift job. Keep the scheduled job read-only and review the drift first; apply on purpose, after looking at plan.

docs.text:

  • Plan, apply, drift: the three commands.
  • JSON output: the report format.

docs.title: Migrate from Ansible
docs.text: Most Ansible playbooks for a single server map onto sadame resource by resource: packages, files, templates, services, users and guarded commands work the same way, with Ruby instead of YAML and ERB instead of Jinja2. This guide translates the ten modules that make up most playbooks, then the inventory, using examples/migrate-from-ansible: an Ansible playbook and its translation, which the test suite applies on Debian and Ubuntu.

docs.title: What is the same, and what is not
docs.text:
Ansible sadame playbook (YAML) recipe (Ruby) hosts: web, --limit -g web, --limit vars:, group_vars, host_vars, -e vars.rb, group and host vars in hosts.rb, --var Jinja2 templates ERB templates with vars and locals notify: and handlers notifies: and subscribes: when: Ruby if loop: Ruby each --check --diff sadame plan no built-in drift command sadame drift become: true sudo: true in hosts.rb, or --sudo Python on every target nothing on the targets; sadame copies itself roles, collections, Galaxy include_recipe and plain Ruby; no package manager for recipes

Tasks run in order in both. A sadame resource reads the current state before acting, as an idempotent Ansible module does; there is no changed_when, because a resource changes exactly when its state differs.

docs.title: The ten common modules
docs.text: Each block shows the Ansible task and its translation from the example.

docs.title: package / apt / dnf
docs.text:
- name: Install packages
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: [nginx, openssl, cron, curl]
        state: present
        update_cache: true

# apt with update_cache: sadame runs apt-get update before the first
# install of a run.
%w[nginx openssl cron curl].each { |name| package name }

package picks apt, dnf, apk or pacman from the distribution, so one recipe covers several families.

docs.title: copy
docs.text:
- name: Login banner
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        dest: /etc/issue.net
        content: "Authorized access only.\n"
        mode: "0644"

    - name: Backup script
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        src: files/backup.sh
        dest: /usr/local/bin/backup
        mode: "0755"

file "/etc/issue.net", content: "Authorized access only.\n", mode: "0644"
file "/usr/local/bin/backup", source: "backup.sh", mode: "0755"

docs.title: template
docs.text:
- name: Site configuration
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: templates/app.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf
        mode: "0644"
      notify: Reload nginx

# Handlers are notifications; delayed, like Ansible's, by default.
file "/etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf",
     template: "app.conf.erb",
     mode: "0644",
     notifies: [:reload, "service[nginx]"]

{{ server_name }} becomes <%= vars[:server_name] %>; {% for %} and {% if %} become <% ... %> with Ruby. See Recipe basics.

docs.title: file
docs.text:
- name: Application directory
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /srv/app
        state: directory
        owner: www-data
        mode: "0755"

    - name: Old configuration is gone
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /etc/nginx/conf.d/old.conf
        state: absent

directory "/srv/app", owner: "www-data", mode: "0755"
file "/etc/nginx/conf.d/old.conf", state: :absent

docs.title: service / systemd
docs.text:
- name: nginx runs and starts at boot
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true

service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

Handlers become the service's notification actions: the handler

  handlers:
    - name: Reload nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: reloaded

is notifies: [:reload, "service[nginx]"] on the file that notified it.

docs.title: user
docs.text:
- name: Deploy user
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: deploy
        shell: /bin/bash
        groups: www-data
        append: true

# groups: always appends, like append: true.
user "deploy", shell: "/bin/bash", groups: ["www-data"]

docs.title: command / shell with creates
docs.text:
- name: Self-signed certificate
      ansible.builtin.command:
        cmd: >-
          openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 365 -subj /CN=app.example.com
          -keyout /etc/ssl/private/app.key -out /etc/ssl/certs/app.crt
        creates: /etc/ssl/private/app.key

exec "openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 365 -subj /CN=app.example.com " \
     "-keyout /etc/ssl/private/app.key -out /etc/ssl/certs/app.crt",
     creates: "/etc/ssl/private/app.key"

creates: is the same; removes: has no equivalent, use only_if: "test -e PATH". A command without a guard runs on every apply in both tools, and sadame's drift always reports it.

docs.title: lineinfile
docs.text:
- name: Default editor
      ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
        path: /etc/environment
        regexp: "^EDITOR="
        line: EDITOR=vim

# No lineinfile: manage the whole file with file, or guard an exec.
exec "echo EDITOR=vim >> /etc/environment", not_if: "grep -q '^EDITOR=vim$' /etc/environment"

sadame has no lineinfile. Prefer managing the whole file with file, so the recipe states what the file contains; for files other programs also edit, a guarded exec as above works.

docs.title: cron
docs.text:
- name: Nightly backup
      ansible.builtin.cron:
        name: backup
        minute: "30"
        hour: "2"
        user: root
        job: /usr/local/bin/backup

file "/etc/cron.d/backup", content: "30 2 * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup\n", mode: "0644"

Ansible's cron edits the user's crontab by default; the translation uses a file in /etc/cron.d, which names the user on each line. See examples/09-cron-and-logrotate.

docs.title: get_url
docs.text:
- name: A page from another server
      ansible.builtin.get_url:
        url: https://www.example.com/
        dest: /srv/app/example.html
        mode: "0644"

exec "curl -fsSL -o /srv/app/example.html https://www.example.com/",
     creates: "/srv/app/example.html"

docs.title: The inventory
docs.text:
An INI inventory:

examples/migrate-from-ansible/ansible/inventory.ini
[web]
web1.example.com
web2.example.com workers=8

[db]
db1.example.com ansible_user=admin ansible_port=2222 ansible_become=true

[web:vars]
workers=4

[all:vars]
env=production

or its YAML form:

examples/migrate-from-ansible/ansible/inventory.yml
all:
  vars:
    env: production
  children:
    web:
      vars:
        workers: 4
      hosts:
        web1.example.com:
        web2.example.com:
          workers: 8
    db:
      hosts:
        db1.example.com:
          ansible_user: admin
          ansible_port: 2222
          ansible_become: true

becomes:

examples/migrate-from-ansible/hosts.rb
# ansible/inventory.ini and ansible/inventory.yml, translated. Ansible's
# all group is implicit; here it is declared, including the other groups.
group :web do
  host "web1.example.com"
  host "web2.example.com", vars: { workers: 8 }
  vars workers: 4
end

group :db do
  host "db1.example.com", user: "admin", port: 2222, sudo: true
end

group :all, include: [:web, :db] do
  vars env: "production"
end
Ansible hosts.rb [web] with host lines group :web do host "..." end ansible_host address: ansible_user, ansible_port user:, port: ansible_become=true sudo: true ansible_ssh_common_args ssh_opts: [web:vars] vars inside the group [all:vars] a group :all that includes the others; Ansible's all is implicit, sadame's is not [app:children] group :app, include: [...] dynamic inventory scripts and plugins Ruby in hosts.rb; see Inventory

Precedence is similar: a host's vars override its groups', and a group's vars override the groups it includes. Ansible has many more layers (role defaults, facts, set_fact); sadame has four, listed on the Inventory page.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
Things Ansible does that sadame 0.1 does not:

  • no facts gathering beyond platform (os-release) and host_name, host_groups;
  • no modules beyond package, file, directory, service, exec and user: no git, apt_repository, mount, sysctl, firewalld and so on; use file and guarded exec (see examples/04-docker-host for a package repository);
  • no Windows, no network devices, no agent or pull mode;
  • no vault; read secrets from the environment in vars.rb;
  • no roles from Galaxy: recipes are files you include_recipe.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Translating shell tasks one to one. Most shell tasks in a playbook exist because a module was missing; check whether a file or package resource says the same thing as state.
  • Forgetting the guard. An exec without creates, not_if or only_if runs every time and makes drift fail.
  • Expecting all to exist. Declare it in hosts.rb if you use it.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Inventory
  • Notifications
  • Comparison with other tools

docs.title: Migrate from Itamae
docs.text: Sadame's recipe language comes from the same family as Itamae's and mitamae's: Ruby files that declare resources, evaluated top to bottom, with templates in ERB. Porting is mostly mechanical: resource names stay, block attributes become keyword options, and node becomes vars. This guide lists what is identical, what changed, and walks through examples/migrate-from-itamae, an Itamae recipe and its translation, which the test suite applies on Debian and Ubuntu.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
Itamaesadame examples/migrate-from-itamae/itamae/recipe.rb
# The Itamae recipe that ../recipe.rb translates, kept for comparison.
# Run with Itamae: itamae local itamae/recipe.rb -j itamae/node.json
package 'nginx'
package 'openssl'

template '/etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf' do
  source 'templates/app.conf.erb'
  mode '644'
  variables(server_name: node[:server_name], workers: node[:workers])
  notifies :reload, 'service[nginx]'
end

directory '/srv/app' do
  owner 'www-data'
  mode '755'
end

remote_file '/usr/local/bin/backup' do
  source 'files/backup.sh'
  mode '755'
end

execute 'self-signed certificate' do
  command 'openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 365 -subj /CN=app.example.com ' \
          '-keyout /etc/ssl/private/app.key -out /etc/ssl/certs/app.crt'
  not_if 'test -f /etc/ssl/private/app.key'
end

user 'deploy' do
  shell '/bin/bash'
end

service 'nginx' do
  action [:enable, :start]
end
examples/migrate-from-itamae/recipe.rb
# itamae/recipe.rb, translated. Resource names mostly stay; blocks become
# keyword options; node becomes vars; template variables become locals.
package "nginx"
package "openssl"

file "/etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf",
     template: "app.conf.erb",
     locals: { server_name: vars[:server_name], workers: vars[:workers] },
     mode: "644",
     notifies: [:reload, "service[nginx]"]

directory "/srv/app", owner: "www-data", mode: "755"

file "/usr/local/bin/backup", source: "backup.sh", mode: "755"

exec "self-signed certificate",
     command: "openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 365 -subj /CN=app.example.com " \
              "-keyout /etc/ssl/private/app.key -out /etc/ssl/certs/app.crt",
     not_if: "test -f /etc/ssl/private/app.key"

user "deploy", shell: "/bin/bash"

service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

The template changes in one way: Itamae's variables(...) arrive as instance variables, sadame's locals: as a Hash.

Itamaesadame examples/migrate-from-itamae/itamae/templates/app.conf.erb
# Managed by Itamae.
server {
  listen 8080;
  server_name <%= @server_name %>;
  root /srv/app;
  # workers: <%= @workers %>
}
examples/migrate-from-itamae/templates/app.conf.erb
# Managed by sadame.
server {
  listen 8080;
  server_name <%= locals[:server_name] %>;
  root /srv/app;
  # workers: <%= locals[:workers] %>
}

docs.title: What is identical
docs.text:
• Recipes are Ruby files evaluated in order; resources run in the order they are declared.
  • package, directory, file, user and service keep their names.
  • include_recipe "path", relative to the including file, each file once.
  • notifies and subscribes, with delayed notifications by default and :immediately.
  • only_if and not_if with shell commands, on exec.
  • Templates are ERB with <%= %>, <% %> and -%>.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
Itamae sadame template "/path" do source "x.erb"; variables(a: 1) end file "/path", template: "x.erb", locals: { a: 1 } remote_file "/path" do source "files/x" end file "/path", source: "x" (looked up next to the recipe, then in files/) execute "name" do command "..." end exec "name", command: "..." service "x" do action [:enable, :start] end service "x", enable: true, state: :running action :nothing action: :nothing, on exec only; service without enable:/state: manages nothing node[:attr], -j node.json, -y node.yml vars[:attr], vars.rb, --var, vars in hosts.rb @name in templates locals[:name]; vars[:name] is also available notifies :reload, "service[x]" notifies: [:reload, "service[x]"] only_if / not_if on any resource on exec only define plain Ruby methods in the recipe run_command in recipes not available; recipes do not run commands while loading mode "644" mode: "644" or "0644"; numbers are rejected itamae local recipe.rb sadame apply recipe.rb itamae ssh -h host recipe.rb sadame apply recipe.rb -h host (copies itself; nothing to install on the host) --dry-run sadame plan no drift command sadame drift

mitamae users: sadame is also a single binary built with mruby, so the mruby limits on recipe code are similar (no gems, no standard library); see Architecture. The differences from mitamae are the same as above, plus push over SSH, inventories and drift.

docs.title: Resources Itamae has and sadame 0.1 does not
docs.text:
link, group, git, http_request, local_ruby_block, gem_package and plugins. Use exec with a guard in the meantime:

docs.title: How to port
docs.text:
1. Move node.json or node.yml values into vars.rb (a Ruby Hash).
  2. Rewrite each resource block as a call with keyword options, using the table above. sadame plan rejects misspelled options with the list of valid ones.
  3. Change @name in templates to locals[:name] or vars[:name].
  4. Move only_if and not_if from non-exec resources into Ruby if around the resource, or into an exec.
  5. Run sadame plan on a machine Itamae already manages. A complete translation shows no changes, or only the differences you expect.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting @variables in templates. They are nil in sadame's templates; use locals[:name].
  • source paths. Itamae paths are relative to the recipe; so are sadame's, but sadame also looks in templates/ and files/, so "templates/x.erb" and "x.erb" both work.
  • Guards on files and packages. Only exec takes only_if and not_if; wrap other resources in Ruby if.
