docs.title: Keep an Omarchy workstation reproducible
docs.text: Omarchy sets up Arch Linux as a complete desktop. What you add on top (packages, dotfiles, a timer or two, something from the AUR) is usually done by hand and remembered by nobody. This guide keeps that layer in a recipe: a fresh Omarchy install plus sadame apply gives the same machine, and sadame drift answers "did I break my laptop?" in one command. It uses examples/12-omarchy-workstation.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
examples/12-omarchy-workstation/recipe.rb
# A personal Arch or Omarchy workstation, applied locally:
#
#   sudo sadame apply examples/12-omarchy-workstation
#
# Packages from the official repositories, dotfiles from files/ into your
# home directory, a systemd user timer, and an AUR package through yay.
# Run `sudo sadame drift ...` now and then: exit 0 means the laptop still
# matches the recipe.
raise "this example is for Arch Linux and Omarchy, not #{platform.description}" unless platform.family == "arch"

me = vars[:user]
raise "run it with sudo, or pass --var user=NAME" if me.nil? || me.empty? || me == "root"

home = "/home/#{me}"

# Packages: only what you want on top of Arch or Omarchy.
vars[:packages].each { |name| package name }

# Dotfiles. Directories are listed so that they belong to you, not root.
["#{home}/.config", "#{home}/.config/systemd", "#{home}/.config/systemd/user", "#{home}/.local",
 "#{home}/.local/bin"].each do |path|
  directory path, owner: me, mode: "0755"
end
file "#{home}/.gitconfig", template: "gitconfig.erb", owner: me, mode: "0644"
file "#{home}/.config/starship.toml", source: "starship.toml", owner: me, mode: "0644"
file "#{home}/.local/bin/update-system", source: "update-system", owner: me, mode: "0755"

# A user timer that empties ~/Downloads of files older than 30 days. Your
# systemd instance must run even when you are logged out, so lingering is
# turned on and the instance started.
exec "enable lingering for #{me}",
     command: "loginctl enable-linger #{me}",
     creates: "/var/lib/systemd/linger/#{me}"
exec "start #{me}'s systemd instance",
     command: "systemctl start user@$(id -u #{me}).service",
     not_if: "systemctl is-active --quiet user@$(id -u #{me}).service"
exec "reload #{me}'s systemd units",
     command: "systemctl --user -M #{me}@ daemon-reload",
     action: :nothing
file "#{home}/.config/systemd/user/clean-downloads.service",
     source: "clean-downloads.service",
     owner: me,
     mode: "0644",
     notifies: [:run, "exec[reload #{me}'s systemd units]", :immediately]
file "#{home}/.config/systemd/user/clean-downloads.timer",
     source: "clean-downloads.timer",
     owner: me,
     mode: "0644",
     notifies: [:run, "exec[reload #{me}'s systemd units]", :immediately]
service "clean-downloads.timer", user: me, enable: true, state: :running

# An AUR package. yay builds as you and asks sudo for pacman, so this needs
# passwordless sudo for pacman or a recent sudo timestamp. Skipped where
# yay is not installed, such as a plain Arch container.
vars[:aur_packages].each do |name|
  exec "install #{name} from the AUR",
       command: "runuser -u #{me} -- yay -S --needed --noconfirm #{name}",
       only_if: "command -v yay",
       not_if: "pacman -Q #{name}"
end
examples/12-omarchy-workstation/vars.rb
# Run with sudo: SUDO_USER is the user whose home directory is managed.
{
  user: ENV["SUDO_USER"],
  git_name: "Your Name",
  git_email: "you@example.com",
  packages: ["git", "htop", "ripgrep", "fd", "bat", "starship"],
  aur_packages: ["visual-studio-code-bin"]
}

Copy the directory somewhere you keep under version control, edit vars.rb and the files in files/ and templates/, and add your own.

docs.title: What belongs in the recipe, and what does not
docs.text:
In the recipe Left to Omarchy packages you install on top of Omarchy the packages Omarchy installs your dotfiles: git identity, shell prompt, editor settings Omarchy's own configuration (Hyprland, Waybar, its themes) your scripts in ~/.local/bin Omarchy's scripts and its update mechanism your systemd user units and timers Omarchy's services AUR packages you rely on yay itself, which Omarchy ships

The rule of thumb: manage what you would have to redo by hand after a reinstall, and leave the files Omarchy installs and updates alone. If the recipe managed them too, every Omarchy update would show up as drift, and every apply would undo the update. When you do change one of Omarchy's settings, make the change the way Omarchy's documentation describes for local changes, so its updates and your recipe do not overwrite each other, and manage only your part.

docs.title: From a fresh install to the same machine
docs.text:
1. Install Omarchy.
  2. Clone the repository with your recipe.
  3. Install sadame (see Install).
  4. sudo sadame apply path/to/your-recipe
  5. sudo sadame drift path/to/your-recipe; exit status 0 means done.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running without sudo, or as root directly. Without sudo, installing packages fails; as root without sudo, SUDO_USER is empty and the recipe stops. Pass --var user=NAME if you must.
  • The AUR step asking for a password. yay runs sudo pacman, and sadame cannot answer a prompt. Run sudo -v just before, or allow pacman without a password.
  • Managing Omarchy's own files. See the table above.
  • Upgrading packages with the recipe. package means "installed", not "latest"; keep updating with pacman -Syu (or update-system from the example).

docs.title: Provision a new VPS
docs.text: This guide takes a freshly created cloud server, the kind Hetzner Cloud or DigitalOcean hands you with only root and your SSH key, to a hardened web server in three sadame apply runs: an administrator account, a security baseline (SSH on port 2222 with keys only, a firewall, fail2ban, automatic updates) and nginx serving a site. Each step is one of the examples, used as it is, and the output below comes from running exactly these commands against a fresh Debian 12 server.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• sadame on your machine (see Install) and a checkout of the repository for the examples, or copies of examples/06-app-deploy-user, examples/07-hardening-baseline and examples/02-nginx-static-site;
  • an SSH key pair; the commands below use ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub;
  • a new server running Debian 12 or Ubuntu 24.04, reachable as root with that key.

docs.title: 1. Create the server
docs.text:
Create it with your public key, in the web console or with the provider's CLI. With Hetzner Cloud's hcloud, after hcloud ssh-key create --name me --public-key-from-file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:

hcloud server create --name vps1 --type cx22 --image debian-12 --ssh-key me   # types: hcloud server-type list

With DigitalOcean's doctl, using the fingerprint from doctl compute ssh-key list:

doctl compute droplet create vps1 --image debian-12-x64 --size s-1vcpu-1gb --region fra1 --ssh-keys FINGERPRINT

Note the server's IP address; the commands below write vps1.example.com in its place. Connect once with ssh root@ADDRESS to check the key works and to accept the host key.

docs.text:

docs.title: Keep it in an inventory
docs.text:
Typing -h deploy@...:2222 --sudo gets old. Put the server in a hosts.rb, as examples/07-hardening-baseline/hosts-after.rb does, and use -g:

examples/07-hardening-baseline/hosts-after.rb
# After the first apply: SSH listens on vars[:ssh_port] (2222) only.
group :new do
  host "vps1.example.com", user: "admin", sudo: true, port: 2222
end

Then Drift in CI checks the server every morning.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running the baseline before the administrator account. The baseline turns off root login; without another user with a key and sudo, you are locked out.
  • Forgetting open_ports. The firewall only lets SSH in. A web server needs --var open_ports=80,443 (or open_ports: [80, 443] in vars.rb).
  • Connecting to port 22 after the baseline. Use HOST:2222, port: 2222 in hosts.rb, or Port 2222 in ~/.ssh/config.
  • The provider's own firewall. Hetzner and DigitalOcean also have firewalls outside the server; open ports 2222, 80 and 443 there too if you use them.

docs.title: Remote hosts
docs.text: With -h, -g or --limit, sadame runs a recipe on other machines over SSH. Nothing has to be installed on them first: sadame copies its own binary and the recipe with your system's scp, runs it with ssh, and shows each host's output as it arrives, prefixed with the host's name. This guide covers how hosts are named and reached, what is copied where, sudo, jump hosts, running many hosts at once, and what to do when a connection fails.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
cd examples/08-multi-role-inventory
sadame plan site.rb -h deploy@db1.example.com:2222

$ sadame plan site.rb -h deploy@db1.example.com:2222

The targets need a POSIX shell, tar with gzip support, sha256sum (or shasum), and Linux or macOS on x86_64 or ARM64. The machine running sadame needs the OpenSSH client (ssh and scp).

docs.title: Naming a host: [user@]host[:port]
docs.text:
Form Meaning web1.example.com user and port from ~/.ssh/config, or ssh's defaults deploy@web1.example.com log in as deploy db1.example.com:2222 connect to port 2222 admin@db1.example.com:2222 both root@[2001:db8::1]:22 IPv6 addresses go in brackets

A name that is also in the inventory keeps the options from there; the user and port given with -h replace those. Several hosts are separated by commas: -h web1.example.com,web2.example.com.

docs.title: SSH configuration and keys
docs.text:
Sadame runs the system's ssh and scp, so everything in ~/.ssh/config applies: HostName, User, Port, IdentityFile, ProxyJump, and the SSH agent. It adds these options to every connection:

Option Why -o BatchMode=yes never stop to ask for a password; use keys or an agent -o ConnectTimeout=10 an unreachable host fails after 10 seconds -o ControlMaster=auto, ControlPath, ControlPersist=60 the several commands of a push share one connection

A host's ssh_opts from hosts.rb come before them, so they can override them; ssh uses the first value it sees for an option. They are passed to scp too, so use options both accept, such as -i, -F, -J and -o.

The first connection to a new host checks its host key against ~/.ssh/known_hosts as usual. With BatchMode, an unknown key is not accepted interactively: connect once with ssh yourself, add the key with ssh-keyscan, or set StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new for those hosts in ~/.ssh/config.

docs.title: Non-standard ports
docs.text:
Any of these works; hosts.rb is the usual place, as for db1 in examples/08-multi-role-inventory/hosts.rb:

host "db1.example.com", port: 2222    # in hosts.rb

sadame plan site.rb -h db1.example.com:2222

Host db1.example.com                  # in ~/.ssh/config
  Port 2222

ssh takes the port with -p and scp with -P; sadame passes the right one to each.

docs.title: Jump hosts
docs.text:
A host that is only reachable through a bastion needs one ProxyJump line in ~/.ssh/config; nothing in sadame changes:

Host app1.internal
  User deploy
  ProxyJump bastion.example.com

To keep that configuration with the recipe instead, put it in a file and pass it with -F through ssh_opts. With -F, ssh reads only that file, so it must also name the key and known hosts file:

host "app1.internal", ssh_opts: ["-F", "ssh_config"]

Sadame's own tests reach a host on a private network through a bastion this way; see test/integration/push/ssh_config and the internal group in test/integration/push/recipe/hosts.rb.

docs.title: sudo
docs.text:
Most recipes need root on the target. Log in as a user with sudo rights and let sadame use sudo, either per host or for every target of a run:

host "web1.example.com", user: "deploy", sudo: true    # in hosts.rb

sadame apply site.rb -g web --sudo                    # every selected host

sudo must not ask for a password, because there is no terminal to type it into. Sadame checks that with sudo -n true before it copies anything. A line like this in /etc/sudoers.d/deploy (edit it with visudo -f) gives the deploy user passwordless sudo:

deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL

docs.title: What is copied where
docs.text:
What Where When The sadame binary for the target's system ~/.sadame/bin/SHA256/sadame on the target only when that checksum is not there yet; it is checked after copying The recipe's directory, without .git, vars.rb and hosts.rb ~/.sadame/run/RUN_ID/ on the target every run; removed when sadame finishes there The target's vars, already merged ~/.sadame/run/RUN_ID/.sadame-vars.rb every run; removed with the directory Binaries downloaded for other systems ~/.sadame/dist/VERSION/ on the machine running sadame the first time a system is needed

vars.rb and hosts.rb are evaluated on the machine running sadame, so ENV and files they read are those of that machine. The target receives the result. Templates and the recipe itself run on the target.

To clean a target, remove ~/.sadame.

docs.title: Where the binary comes from
docs.text:
Sadame needs a binary for each target's system (uname -sm on the target). It looks in this order:

  1. $SADAME_BINARY_DIR/sadame-linux-amd64 (and so on), if that variable is set; useful for development builds and machines without internet access: SADAME_BINARY_DIR=dist;
  2. itself, when it is the binary for that system (a Linux x86_64 machine pushing to Linux x86_64 targets copies itself);
  3. ~/.sadame/dist/VERSION/, from an earlier download;
  4. the GitHub release of the same version, checked against its SHA256SUMS; $SADAME_DOWNLOAD_URL points at a mirror instead.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting password prompts. Sadame never asks for SSH or sudo passwords. Use keys and passwordless sudo.
  • Recipes in a large directory. The recipe's whole directory is copied to every host on every run. Keep recipes in their own directory, not at the top of a large repository.
  • Reading local files in a recipe. A recipe runs on the target; a path like ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub there means the target's file. Put files the recipe needs next to it and use source:.
  • Pushing to a target with a different sadame version installed. That does not matter: sadame always runs the binary it copied, identified by its checksum.

docs.title: Team workflow
docs.text: When several people change the same servers, sadame works best with the same habits as application code: recipes and the inventory in git, changes through pull requests, the plan reviewed before anything is applied, and a scheduled drift check that tells you when a server no longer matches the repository. This guide sets that up with the pipelines in examples/ci/.

docs.title: The repository
docs.text:
Keep everything sadame reads in one repository:

infrastructure/
  site/
    site.rb            # entry point; includes roles by host_groups
    hosts.rb           # the inventory
    vars.rb            # defaults
    roles/web.rb, roles/db.rb, roles/templates/...
  .github/workflows/
    plan.yml           # plan on every pull request
    apply.yml          # apply after merging, with approval
    drift.yml          # drift every morning

examples/08-multi-role-inventory has this shape. Secrets do not go in the repository: read them from the environment in vars.rb (ENV["DB_PASSWORD"]) and set them in the CI secrets; mark files that hold them sensitive: true so their content does not appear in plans.

docs.title: Review the plan, not only the code
docs.text:
A recipe change is easier to review with its effect next to it. This pipeline runs sadame plan against every server on each pull request and puts the output on the run's summary page:

examples/ci/github-actions-plan.yml
# Shows what a pull request would change on every server: runs `sadame plan`
# against the inventory and puts the output on the run's summary page, next
# to the code being reviewed. It changes nothing.
#
# Copy to .github/workflows/plan.yml. It needs the same secrets as
# github-actions-drift.yml: SSH_PRIVATE_KEY and SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS.
name: Plan

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["site/**"]

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install sadame
        run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enderkus/sadame/main/install.sh | sh

      - name: Set up SSH
        run: |
          install -d -m 0700 ~/.ssh
          printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
          chmod 0600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
          printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS }}" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts

      - name: Plan every server
        run: |
          set -o pipefail
          sadame plan site/site.rb -g all --no-color | tee plan.txt

      - name: Put the plan on the summary page
        if: always()
        run: |
          {
            echo '## sadame plan'
            echo '```'
            cat plan.txt
            echo '```'
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

Reviewers then see, per host, the diff of every file the change touches, packages to install, services to restart. A plan that shows more than the author expected is the most useful thing a review can find. Like any command it can only show what differs from the servers as they are now; if someone changes a server by hand between the plan and the apply, the drift check catches it.

docs.title: Who runs apply
docs.text:
Pick one and write it down:

Model How Suits Humans, after review a maintainer runs sadame apply site/site.rb -g ... from their machine once the pull request is merged small teams, few servers, changes that need watching CI, after approval the pipeline below, gated by a GitHub environment with required reviewers teams that want a record of who applied what, and when examples/ci/github-actions-apply.yml
# Applies the recipe to every server after a change is merged, once someone
# approves the run. The approval comes from the "production" environment:
# create it under Settings > Environments and add required reviewers.
#
# Copy to .github/workflows/apply.yml. It needs the same secrets as
# github-actions-drift.yml: SSH_PRIVATE_KEY and SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS.
name: Apply

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["site/**"]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  apply:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    # Never two applies at once; a newer one waits for the running one.
    concurrency:
      group: apply
      cancel-in-progress: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install sadame
        run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enderkus/sadame/main/install.sh | sh

      - name: Set up SSH
        run: |
          install -d -m 0700 ~/.ssh
          printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
          chmod 0600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
          printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS }}" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts

      - name: Apply to every server
        run: sadame apply site/site.rb -g all --no-color

concurrency makes sure two applies never run at once. In both models, apply from the main branch only, so the servers match what is in git.

docs.title: Check for drift on a schedule
docs.text: The third pipeline runs sadame drift every morning and fails when a server differs from the recipe; Drift in CI explains it. When it fails, either the server was changed by hand (apply to put it back, after finding out why) or the change was intended (move it into the recipe with a pull request).

docs.title: Conventions that help
docs.text:
• Small pull requests. One concern per change keeps the plan readable.
  • Run sadame hosts when changing the inventory. It shows which hosts a selection reaches and where each var comes from.
  • Use --limit to roll out gradually. Apply to --limit "web1*" first, then the rest.
  • Keep exec resources guarded. An unguarded exec shows up in every plan and makes every drift check fail, which trains people to ignore both.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Applying from a branch. The servers then match code nobody merged; the next apply from main undoes it.
  • Reviewing only the recipe diff. A one-line change to a shared template can change files on every host; the plan shows it.
  • Ignoring drift failures. A drift check that is always red gets muted; fix the cause or the recipe the same day.

docs.title: Recipe basics
docs.text: A recipe is a Ruby file that declares the desired state of a machine as a list of resources. Sadame evaluates the file from top to bottom, collects the resources in the order they appear, and then plans or applies them in that order. Because the recipe is ordinary Ruby, loops, conditionals and helper methods need no special syntax. This page covers how a recipe directory is laid out, where vars come from, how include_recipe splits a recipe into files, and how templates work.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
The example used on this page lives in examples/basics:

examples/basics/
  recipe.rb                 # entry point
  vars.rb                   # default vars
  parts/motd.rb             # included recipe
  parts/templates/motd.erb  # template used by parts/motd.rb
examples/basics/recipe.rb
# Packages every machine in this example gets. vars come from vars.rb and
# --var; a recipe is plain Ruby, so a loop is just a loop.
vars[:base_packages].each do |name|
  package name
end

directory "/etc/sadame-demo", mode: "0755"

# Paths in include_recipe are relative to this file; ".rb" is optional.
include_recipe "parts/motd"
examples/basics/vars.rb
# vars.rb is plain Ruby; its last expression must be a Hash.
{
  team: "platform",
  contact: "ops@example.com",
  base_packages: ["curl", "less"],
  maintenance: nil
}
examples/basics/parts/motd.rb
# Templates are looked up next to this file, then in its templates/ directory.
file "/etc/motd", template: "motd.erb", mode: "0644"
examples/basics/parts/templates/motd.erb
This machine is managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
Team:    <%= vars[:team] %>
Contact: <%= vars[:contact] %>
<% if vars[:maintenance] -%>

<% end -%>

docs.title: The recipe file
docs.text:
• Each resource is a method call: type "name", option: value, .... The name identifies the resource: a package name, a path, a command, a user name. Together they form the resource id, type[name], which shows up in output and is used by notifies:.
  • An id may appear only once. Declaring package "git" twice is an error that names the file and line.
  • Options are checked when the recipe loads. A misspelled option fails the whole run, with exit status 2, before anything is changed:
$ sudo sadame plan
sadame: recipe.rb:2: file[/etc/motd]: unknown option :contents (valid options: content, group, locals, mode, notifies, owner, sensitive, source, state, subscribes, template)

$ echo $?
2
  • Ruby code in a recipe runs every time the recipe is loaded, for plan as well as apply. Use it to decide what to declare; make changes only through resources.

Besides the resources, a recipe can use:

Name What it is vars Hash of variables with symbol keys (see below) platform.family "debian", "rhel", "alpine", "arch" or nil platform.package_manager "apt", "dnf", "apk", "pacman" or nil platform.id, platform.version, platform.codename, platform.name ID, VERSION_ID, VERSION_CODENAME and PRETTY_NAME from /etc/os-release host_name, host_groups the host's name and groups from the inventory; see Inventory include_recipe "path" evaluate another recipe file

For example, a package whose name differs between distributions:

examples/resources/package/by_family.rb
# Package names are the distribution's own; pick one with plain Ruby.
web_server = platform.family == "debian" ? "apache2" : "httpd"
package web_server

docs.title: vars
docs.text:
vars is a plain Hash with symbol keys. In this release it is filled from two places, highest precedence first:

Precedence Source Example 1 (highest) --var key=value on the command line, repeatable --var workers=8 2 vars.rb next to the recipe { workers: 4 }

vars.rb is Ruby whose last expression is a Hash; it can compute values, for example read an environment variable. Keys may be symbols or strings and always become symbols.

Values given with --var are strings, except:

Given Becomes true, false true, false digits with an optional leading -, and no leading zero Integer: 8, -2, 0 anything else String: "0644", "1.5", "web01"

docs.title: include_recipe
docs.text:
include_recipe "parts/motd" evaluates parts/motd.rb. The path is relative to the file that contains the call, and .rb is optional. The included file shares vars and adds its resources at that point in the order. A file included more than once is evaluated only the first time, so two roles can both include a common base recipe.

Templates and source files used by an included recipe are looked up relative to that file, not the entry point. That keeps a directory such as parts/ or roles/web/ self-contained.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
file with template: renders an ERB template. Sadame implements the commonly used part of ERB itself, because the single binary cannot ship Ruby's ERB library:

Tag Effect <%= expression %> inserts the result of expression <% code %> runs Ruby code: if, each, assignments <%# comment %> produces nothing -%> at the end of any tag: also removes the newline that follows <%- at the start of a tag: also removes the indentation before it <%% a literal <%

Inside a template, vars is the run's vars and locals is the Hash given to the file resource's locals: option. Nothing else from the recipe is visible.

The template is looked up in the recipe's directory first, then in its templates/ subdirectory. parts/motd.rb above uses motd.erb, found at parts/templates/motd.erb.

After apply, changing a var shows exactly which lines of the rendered file change:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/basics --var contact=platform@example.com
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ file[/etc/motd]

    +++ /etc/motd (desired)
    @@ -1,3 +1,3 @@

     Team:    platform
    -Contact: ops@example.com
    +Contact: platform@example.com

Plan: 0 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 3 unchanged.

An error in a template fails that resource and names the template and line. Here templates/app.conf.erb contains port = <%= port %>:

x file[/etc/app.conf]
    error: templates/app.conf.erb:3: undefined method 'port' for Sadame::Template::Scope

Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged, 1 failed.

$ echo $?
2

Here the template used port instead of locals[:port]. The wording after the line number comes from the Ruby runtime and differs slightly between the single binary and CRuby.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• String keys in vars. Keys are always symbols: vars[:team], not vars["team"], which returns nil.
  • Blank lines from control tags. <% if x %> on its own line leaves an empty line in the output, as in ERB. End such tags with -%>.
  • Expecting --var port=08080 to be a number. Leading zeros keep a value a string, so modes like 0644 survive.
  • Side effects in Ruby code. File.write or backticks at the top of a recipe run during plan too. Use exec with a guard instead.
  • Templates next to the wrong file. A template used in roles/web.rb belongs in roles/ or roles/templates/, not next to the entry recipe.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text: An inventory lists the machines a recipe runs on, groups them, and gives groups and hosts their own vars and connection options. It is a file named hosts.rb next to the recipe (or any file passed with --inventory), and like a recipe it is plain Ruby: a static list is a few host lines, and a dynamic inventory is code that calls host in a loop over data from a file or a cloud provider's CLI. There is no plugin system to learn.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/08-multi-role-inventory/hosts.rb
# Three servers in two roles. The names are placeholders: replace them with
# yours, or point them at real machines in ~/.ssh/config.
group :web do
  host "web1.example.com", user: "deploy", sudo: true
  host "web2.example.com", user: "deploy", sudo: true, vars: { workers: 8 }
  vars workers: 4, server_name: "www.example.com"
end

group :db do
  # sshd listens on a non-standard port here.
  host "db1.example.com", user: "deploy", port: 2222, sudo: true
  vars backup_hour: 3
end

group :all, include: [:web, :db] do
  vars env: "production"
end

sadame hosts shows what sadame makes of it: every host, how it will be reached, and each var with the layer it came from:

$ sadame hosts

  sudo      yes
  ssh_opts  (none)
  groups    web, all
  vars
    env          "production"       group all
    workers      4                  group web
    server_name  "www.example.com"  group web
    backup_hour  1                  vars.rb

web2.example.com
  address   web2.example.com
  user      deploy
  port      (ssh default)
  sudo      yes
  ssh_opts  (none)
  groups    web, all
  vars
    env          "production"       group all
    workers      8                  host
    server_name  "www.example.com"  group web
    backup_hour  1                  vars.rb

db1.example.com
  address   db1.example.com
  user      deploy
  port      2222
  sudo      yes
  ssh_opts  (none)
  groups    db, all
  vars
    env          "production"  group all
    workers      2             vars.rb
    server_name  "localhost"   vars.rb
    backup_hour  3             group db

docs.title: The hosts.rb language
docs.text:
Method Where Meaning group :name do ... end top level Declares a group, or adds to one declared earlier. Groups cannot be nested. group :name, include: [:a, :b] top level The group also contains every host of groups a and b. The block is optional. host "name", options in a group, or top level for an ungrouped host Declares a host. A host may appear in several groups. vars key: value, ... in a group Vars for every host of the group. command_output("command") anywhere Runs a command on the machine running sadame and returns its output; fails when the command fails.

JSON.parse and File.read are available, as in recipes.

Options of host:

Option Type Default Meaning address String the host's name Address to connect to, when the name is only a label. user String ssh's default (~/.ssh/config or your user name) User to log in as. port Integer ssh's default (~/.ssh/config or 22) SSH port. sudo true or false false Run sadame with sudo on this host. ssh_opts Array of Strings [] Extra options for ssh and scp, such as ["-i", "~/.ssh/deploy"] or ["-F", "ssh_config"]. vars Hash {} Vars for this host only.

Connection options may be given in any one declaration of a host. Giving the same option two different values is an error; vars from several declarations are merged.

docs.title: Vars precedence
docs.text:
Every target gets one vars Hash, merged from these layers. A higher layer wins for the same key:

Precedence Layer Shown by sadame hosts as 1 (highest) --var key=value on the command line --var 2 vars: of the host host 3 vars of the host's groups; a group overrides the groups it includes, and otherwise a group declared later overrides one declared earlier group NAME 4 (lowest) vars.rb next to the recipe vars.rb

In the example, workers is 2 in vars.rb, 4 for the web group and 8 for web2; env is "staging" in vars.rb but "production" from all, which includes web and db. --var overrides all of them:

$ sadame hosts --limit web2.example.com --var workers=16
sadame 0.1.0.dev hosts: 1 host from hosts.rb

web2.example.com
  address   web2.example.com
  user      deploy
  port      (ssh default)
  sudo      yes
  ssh_opts  (none)
  groups    web, all
  vars
    env          "production"       group all
    workers      16                 --var
    server_name  "www.example.com"  group web
    backup_hour  1                  vars.rb

docs.title: Selecting hosts
docs.text:
Without -h, -g or --limit, sadame runs on the machine it is started on. With any of them, it runs on the selected hosts over SSH (see Remote hosts).

Flag Selects -g web,db the hosts of these groups, including groups they include -h web1.example.com,admin@db9.example.com:2200 these hosts; a name found in the inventory keeps its options, with user and port from the flag when given; any other name works too --limit "web*" only the selected hosts whose name matches the pattern (* any characters, ? one); alone, it filters every host of the inventory

Flags combine: -g db -h web1.example.com selects both, and -g all --limit "web*" narrows all down to the web servers. Hosts are taken in the order of the groups given, then the -h hosts; each runs once. sadame hosts accepts the same flags, which makes it the way to check a selection before running anything.

docs.title: Using groups in recipes
docs.text:
A recipe learns the groups of the host it runs on from host_groups, a list of symbols that includes groups reached through include:. The example's site.rb picks roles that way:

examples/08-multi-role-inventory/site.rb
# Every host gets the base below; the roles follow the host's groups in
# hosts.rb. Run it on all of them with: sadame apply site.rb -g all
file "/etc/motd", template: "motd.erb", locals: { name: host_name, groups: host_groups }

include_recipe "roles/web" if host_groups.include?(:web)
include_recipe "roles/db" if host_groups.include?(:db)

host_name is the host's name from the inventory or -h. For local runs they are "local" and [], unless set with --host-name and --host-groups, which is a way to try a role on a test machine:

sudo sadame plan site.rb --host-groups web,all

docs.title: From a file
docs.text:
examples/11-dynamic-inventory/hosts.rb
# A dynamic inventory: hosts.rb is Ruby, so it can build the host list from
# any data. This one reads servers.json, which another tool might write.
# Paths are relative to where you run sadame, so build them from __FILE__.
servers = JSON.parse(File.read(File.join(File.dirname(__FILE__), "servers.json")))

servers.group_by { |server| server["role"] }.each do |role, members|
  group role.to_sym do
    members.each do |server|
      options = { address: server["address"], user: "deploy" }
      options[:port] = server["port"] if server["port"]
      host server["name"], options
    end
  end
end

group :all, include: [:web, :db] do
  vars env: "production"
end

  { "name": "db1.example.com", "address": "203.0.113.21", "role": "db", "port": 2222 }
]

docs.title: From a cloud provider's CLI
docs.text:
command_output runs the provider's CLI on the machine running sadame, with whatever login that CLI already has. These three files are in the example directory; pass one with --inventory.

Hetzner Cloud (hcloud)DigitalOcean (doctl)AWS (aws) examples/11-dynamic-inventory/hosts-hcloud.rb
# Hetzner Cloud: every server, grouped by its "role" label.
#   sadame hosts --inventory hosts-hcloud.rb
servers = JSON.parse(command_output("hcloud server list -o json"))

servers.each do |server|
  role = server["labels"]["role"] || "unassigned"
  group role.to_sym do
    host server["name"], address: server["public_net"]["ipv4"]["ip"], user: "root"
  end
end
examples/11-dynamic-inventory/hosts-doctl.rb
# DigitalOcean: every Droplet, in one group per tag.
#   sadame hosts --inventory hosts-doctl.rb
droplets = JSON.parse(command_output("doctl compute droplet list --output json"))

droplets.each do |droplet|
  public_ip = droplet["networks"]["v4"].find { |network| network["type"] == "public" }
  next if public_ip.nil?

  droplet["tags"].each do |tag|
    group tag.to_sym do
      host droplet["name"], address: public_ip["ip_address"], user: "root"
    end
  end
end
examples/11-dynamic-inventory/hosts-aws.rb
# AWS EC2: running instances, named and grouped by their Name and Role tags.
#   sadame hosts --inventory hosts-aws.rb
reply = JSON.parse(command_output("aws ec2 describe-instances " \
                                  "--filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running --output json"))

reply["Reservations"].each do |reservation|
  reservation["Instances"].each do |instance|
    tags = {}
    (instance["Tags"] || []).each { |tag| tags[tag["Key"]] = tag["Value"] }
    next if instance["PublicIpAddress"].nil?

    role = (tags["Role"] || "unassigned").to_sym
    group role do
      host tags["Name"] || instance["InstanceId"], address: instance["PublicIpAddress"], user: "ec2-user"
    end
  end
end

The tests run each of them against recorded CLI output, so a change in sadame that breaks them is noticed. A change in a CLI's output format is not; check sadame hosts --inventory ... after upgrading the CLI.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Relative paths in hosts.rb. File.read("servers.json") is relative to the directory you run sadame from. Build paths from File.dirname(__FILE__), as the example does.
  • vars outside a group. Top-level vars is an error; use vars.rb for defaults and host ..., vars: {} for one host.
  • Expecting -g all without a group named all. Groups are only what hosts.rb declares. sadame hosts without flags lists every host.
  • Slow commands in a dynamic inventory. command_output runs every time the inventory loads, including for plan. Cache the result in a file if the CLI is slow.
  • Secrets in hosts.rb. It is evaluated on the machine running sadame, and its vars are sent to the targets. Read secrets from the environment (ENV["DB_PASSWORD"]) rather than committing them.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: A notification runs an action on one resource because another resource changed: reload nginx after its configuration file changed, run systemctl daemon-reload after a unit file changed, restart a service when its settings changed. Nothing is triggered when the watched resource was already as the recipe wants it, so a service is only restarted when there is a reason to. By default a notified action runs once, at the end of apply, however many resources asked for it; marked :immediately, it runs right after the change that triggered it.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/service/reload_on_change.rb
# Reload nginx when its configuration changes. The reload runs once, at the
# end of apply, and only if the file changed.
package "nginx"

file "/etc/nginx/conf.d/status.conf",
     content: "server {\n  listen 127.0.0.1:8080;\n  location = /status { stub_status; }\n}\n",
     mode: "0644",
     notifies: [:reload, "service[nginx]"]

service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Both options are available on every resource.

Option Form Meaning notifies [:action, "type[name]"] When this resource changes, run action on the named resource. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"] When the named resource changes, run action on this resource. either [:action, "type[name]", :immediately] Run the action right after the change instead of at the end. either [:action, "type[name]", :delayed] The default, written out. either [[...], [...]] Several notifications from one resource.

subscribes is notifies declared from the other side; use whichever reads better. Actions each resource type accepts:

Resource Actions service :start, :stop, :restart, :reload, :enable, :disable exec :run package, file, directory, user none

exec also takes action: :nothing: the command then never runs on its own, only when notified. That is the usual way to write "run this after that changed".

docs.title: How notifications run
docs.text:
• Only a resource that changed during apply triggers its notifications. Unchanged, failed and skipped resources trigger nothing.
  • Delayed notifications (the default) run after the last resource, in the order they were first triggered. Each action on each resource runs once: if three configuration files ask to restart nginx, it restarts once.
  • Immediate notifications run right after the resource that triggered them, every time they are triggered, before the next resource is looked at.
  • If a resource fails, the run stops: later resources are skipped and delayed notifications do not run. A failed immediate notification stops the run in the same way.
  • plan and drift never run notifications. They list, under each resource that would change, what it would trigger.
  • Every notification must name a declared resource and an action it supports. Mistakes are reported when the recipe loads, before anything runs.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
The example below manages a small systemd service together with its unit file and settings:

examples/notifications/recipe.rb
# A small systemd service whose unit file and settings are managed here.
# Notifications keep the running process in step with those files.

# Runs only when notified.
exec "systemctl daemon-reload", action: :nothing

# systemd must re-read a changed unit file before the service below is
# started or restarted, so daemon-reload runs immediately. The restart can
# wait until the end of the run.
file "/etc/systemd/system/ticker.service",
     template: "ticker.service.erb",
     mode: "0644",
     notifies: [
       [:run, "exec[systemctl daemon-reload]", :immediately],
       [:restart, "service[ticker]"]
     ]

# Settings the service reads when it starts.
file "/etc/default/ticker", content: "INTERVAL=#{vars[:interval]}\n", mode: "0644"

# The service asks to be restarted when its settings change; this is the
# same as notifies: on the file above, declared from the other side.
service "ticker",
        enable: true,
        state: :running,
        subscribes: [:restart, "file[/etc/default/ticker]"]
examples/notifications/templates/ticker.service.erb
# Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
[Unit]
Description=<%= vars[:description] %>

[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/etc/default/ticker
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'while true; do date >> /var/log/ticker.log; sleep ${INTERVAL}; done'

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
examples/notifications/vars.rb
{
  interval: 60,
  description: "Writes the date to /var/log/ticker.log"
}

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Delayed daemon-reload. systemctl daemon-reload after a unit file change must happen before the service is started or restarted. Mark it :immediately; a delayed reload runs after the restart it was meant to prepare.
  • An exec without action: :nothing. A notified exec that also has no guard runs on every apply anyway, and drift always reports it.
  • Reloading a unit that cannot reload. systemctl reload fails for units without ExecReload=; notify :restart instead.
  • Expecting a notification after a failed run. Delayed notifications are skipped when a resource fails. Fix the failure and apply again; the resource that changed earlier is now unchanged and will not notify again, so restart by hand if needed.
  • Typos in the target. "service[ngnix]" is reported when the recipe loads: file[/etc/nginx/nginx.conf] notifies service[ngnix], which is not declared.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text: plan, apply and drift print a single JSON document with --json, instead of the human-readable report. It contains everything the text report shows: each resource's status and changes, the notifications, the summary counts, and the exit status. Nothing else is written to standard output, so it can be redirected to a file or piped into jq. Errors that stop sadame before a report exists (a bad option, a recipe that does not load) go to standard error, and standard output stays empty.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: Field Type Description format_version integer Version of this format, currently 1. It changes when a field is removed or changes meaning; new fields may be added without a change. sadame_version string Version of sadame that wrote the report. command string "plan", "apply" or "drift". host string The machine the report is about; "local" for the machine sadame runs on. platform object See platform. resources array One resource object per declared resource, in recipe order. notifications array Notification runs during apply, in the order they ran. Always empty for plan and drift. summary object Number of resources per status; see statuses. Every status of the command is present, including those with 0. drift boolean or null plan and drift: true when at least one resource differs from the recipe. apply: null. failed boolean true when a resource failed, or for apply, a notification failed. exit_status integer The exit status of the command: see Plan, apply, drift. duration_seconds number Wall-clock time of the run, rounded to hundredths of a second.

docs.title: platform
docs.text: Field Type Description name string PRETTY_NAME from /etc/os-release, or "macOS". family string or null "debian", "rhel", "alpine", "arch", or null when unknown. package_manager string or null "apt", "dnf", "apk", "pacman", or null.

docs.title: resource
docs.text: Field Type Description id string type[name], as in the text output and in notifies:. type string "package", "file", "directory", "service", "exec" or "user". name string The resource name: package name, path, command, user name. status string See statuses. changes array Change objects. Empty when the resource is unchanged, failed before comparing, or skipped. notifications array plan and drift: what this resource would trigger. apply: what it triggered. Each has action, source, target and timing ("delayed" or "immediately"). error string or null Why the resource failed, or null.

docs.title: change
docs.text:
An attribute that differs. Most changes have from and to:

Field Type Description attribute string "state", "mode", "owner", "group", "enabled", "uid", "home", "shell", "groups" or "command". from string, integer, boolean, array or null Current value; null when the resource does not exist yet. to same Desired value. reason string Only on exec changes: why the command would run, for example "not_if exited non-zero".

File content changes carry a diff instead of the full text:

Field Type Description attribute string "content" sensitive boolean true when the file has sensitive: true. diff string or null Unified diff from current to desired, or null when sensitive.

docs.title: notification run
docs.text: Field Type Description action string The action, such as "reload" or "run". source string Id of the resource whose change triggered it. target string Id of the resource the action ran on. timing string "delayed" or "immediately". status string "ok" or "failed". error string or null Why it failed, or null.

docs.title: Statuses
docs.text: Command Status Meaning plan, drift create Does not exist yet. update Exists, some attributes differ. remove Exists, the recipe says state: :absent. run An exec whose guards say it must run. unchanged Matches the recipe. failed The current state could not be read; see error. apply changed Was changed. unchanged Already matched; nothing was done. failed Changing it failed; see error. skipped Not looked at, because an earlier resource or immediate notification failed.

docs.title: Push mode
docs.text:
When sadame runs on remote hosts (-h, -g, --limit), --json prints one document for the whole run. Each host's report, as described above, is nested under hosts:

docs.text:
• Reading failed as "drift found". failed means a resource could not be checked or changed. Drift is the drift field, and the exit status 1.

docs.title: directory
docs.text: directory makes sure a directory exists, with the permission bits and owner you give, or that it does not exist. Missing parent directories are created along the way. Use it before file resources that write into a new directory, and to keep application directories owned by the right user.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/directory/minimal.rb
directory "/srv/app"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description mode String of 3 or 4 octal digits unmanaged Permission bits, such as "0755". owner String unmanaged User name that owns the directory. group String unmanaged Group name of the directory. state :present or :absent :present :absent removes the directory. recursive true or false false With state: :absent, remove the directory and everything in it (rm -rf). Without it, only an empty directory can be removed (rmdir). notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

Creating runs mkdir -p, then chmod and chown for the attributes you gave. Parents created by mkdir -p get default permissions; declare them as their own resources if they matter.

docs.text:
examples/resources/directory/recipe.rb
directory "/srv/app", mode: "0755"
directory "/srv/app/shared", owner: "www-data", group: "www-data", mode: "0750"

# Remove a directory and everything in it.
directory "/srv/app/tmp", state: :absent, recursive: true

docs.title: Removing a directory
docs.text: The last resource in the recipe removes /srv/app/tmp and everything in it whenever it shows up. Without recursive: true, removing a directory that still has files in it fails with rmdir's error, which protects you from deleting more than you meant to.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Owner that does not exist yet. owner: "www-data" fails if the user is created later in the recipe, or by a package declared after the directory. Order the package or user resource first.
  • A file in the way. If the path exists as a regular file, the resource fails with "is a regular file, not a directory"; sadame does not delete it for you.
  • Expecting mode to apply to the contents. Only the directory itself is changed, never the files inside.

docs.title: exec
docs.text: exec runs a shell command. It is the escape hatch for anything the other resources do not cover: issuing a certificate, running an installer, installing from the AUR. A command has no state sadame can read, so to stay idempotent an exec needs a guard that says when the work is already done. Guards are evaluated during plan as well as apply; the command itself only runs during apply.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/exec/minimal.rb
exec "tar -czf /var/backups/etc.tar.gz /etc", creates: "/var/backups/etc.tar.gz"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description command String the resource name Command to run, when you want the name to be a short label. creates String none Skip when this path exists. not_if String none Skip when this command exits 0. only_if String none Skip unless this command exits 0. cwd String inherited Working directory for the command and its guards. env Hash of String to String none Environment variables for the command and its guards. action :run or :nothing :run :nothing never runs the command on its own, only when another resource notifies it. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this command runs. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

The command runs when every guard you gave agrees: the creates path is missing, not_if exits non-zero, and only_if exits 0. Guards are checked in that order and checking stops at the first one that says skip. Without any guard, the command runs on every apply.

Commands and guards run with /bin/sh and standard input closed. A command that exits non-zero fails the resource: apply prints the exit status and the command's error output, marks the resource failed, and skips the resources after it.

Other resources can trigger the command with notifies: [:run, "exec[NAME]"]. Combined with action: :nothing, that gives a command that runs only when something else changed, such as systemctl daemon-reload after a unit file changed; see Notifications.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/exec/recipe.rb
directory "/opt/demo"

# creates: skip when the path exists.
exec "tar -czf /opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz -C /etc hostname hosts",
     creates: "/opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz"

# not_if: skip when the command succeeds.
exec "echo 'EDITOR=vim' >> /etc/environment",
     not_if: "grep -qs '^EDITOR=vim$' /etc/environment"

# only_if: run only when the command succeeds. Here: only on hosts with git,
# and only until the setting is in place.
exec "git config --system init.defaultBranch main",
     only_if: "command -v git",
     not_if: "git config --system --get init.defaultBranch"

# cwd: and env: set the working directory and environment.
exec "echo \"built by $BUILDER\" > build-info.txt",
     cwd: "/opt/demo",
     env: { "BUILDER" => "sadame" },
     creates: "/opt/demo/build-info.txt"

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No guard. An exec without creates, not_if or only_if runs on every apply, plan always lists it with "(no guard, runs on every apply)", and drift always reports it. Add a guard, or use action: :nothing if it should only run when notified.
  • Guards with side effects. Guards run during plan. A guard such as not_if: "mkdir /x" changes the machine when you only asked to look.
  • Interactive commands. Standard input is closed, so a command that prompts reads end-of-file and usually fails. Pass the tool's non-interactive flag (-y, --noconfirm).
  • A guard that never becomes true. If the command does not create what the guard checks for, it runs every time. Check the exact path or setting the command produces.

docs.text:
• package for installing AUR packages with exec.
  • Recipe basics for using vars in commands.

docs.title: file
docs.text: file manages a regular file: its content, permission bits and owner. The content comes from a string, an ERB template, or a file shipped next to the recipe. When the content differs, plan shows a unified diff of the file on disk against the desired content. On apply, new content is written to a temporary file in the same directory, given its final mode and owner, and renamed over the target, so programs reading the file never see it half written.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/file/minimal.rb
file "/etc/motd", content: "Authorized access only.\n"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description content String none The exact file content. template String none ERB template, rendered with vars and locals. Looked up next to the recipe, then in its templates/ directory. Absolute paths are used as is. source String none File copied as is. Looked up next to the recipe, then in its files/ directory. locals Hash {} Values for the template, available as locals[:name]. Only with template:. mode String of 3 or 4 octal digits unmanaged Permission bits, such as "0644" or "0755". owner String unmanaged User name that owns the file. group String unmanaged Group name of the file. state :present or :absent :present :absent deletes the file. sensitive true or false false Hide content diffs in output and JSON, for files holding secrets. verify String containing %{path} none A command that checks the new content before it replaces the file, such as "visudo -cf %{path}". %{path} is the temporary file. If the command fails, the file is left as it was and the resource fails. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

Use at most one of content, template and source. With none of them, sadame manages only the attributes you give and creates an empty file if it is missing. Attributes you do not give are left alone; when the content is replaced, the file keeps its current mode, owner and group.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
The recipe used below:

examples/resources/file/recipe.rb
# Inline content.
file "/etc/issue.net", content: "Authorized access only.\n", mode: "0644"

# A template, rendered with vars (from vars.rb or --var) and locals.
directory "/etc/hello"
file "/etc/hello/hello.conf",
     template: "hello.conf.erb",
     locals: { port: 8080 },
     mode: "0640",
     owner: "root",
     group: "root"

# A file copied as is from the files/ directory.
file "/usr/local/bin/hello", source: "hello.sh", mode: "0755"

# Make sure a file does not exist.
file "/etc/hello/old.conf", state: :absent
examples/resources/file/templates/hello.conf.erb
# Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
listen = <%= locals[:port] %>
environment = <%= vars[:environment] %>
<% vars[:upstreams].each do |upstream| -%>
upstream = <%= upstream %>
<% end -%>

{
  environment: "staging",
  upstreams: ["10.0.0.11:9000", "10.0.0.12:9000"]
}

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Numeric modes. mode: 644 is rejected. Ruby reads 644 as decimal, which is not the mode you mean; write mode: "0644".
  • Symlinks. If the path is a symbolic link, the resource fails with "is a symbolic link, not a regular file" instead of replacing the link. Manage the link's target path instead.
  • Missing parent directory. file does not create parent directories. Declare a directory resource before it.
  • Secrets in plan output. Without sensitive: true, the diff of a file holding credentials is printed and included in --json output.
  • Unchecked configuration files. A broken sudoers or sshd file can lock you out of a server. Give such files verify:; see examples/06-app-deploy-user.
  • Template next to the wrong recipe. Templates are found relative to the recipe file that declares the resource; see Recipe basics.

docs.title: package
docs.text: package makes sure a system package is installed, or not installed. Sadame reads /etc/os-release to pick the package manager, so the same recipe works on Debian and Ubuntu (apt), Rocky, AlmaLinux and Fedora (dnf), Alpine (apk), and Arch and Arch-based systems such as Omarchy (pacman). Before acting it asks the package manager whether the package is installed, and only installs or removes when the answer differs from the recipe.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/package/minimal.rb
package "htop"

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description state :installed or :absent :installed Whether the package must be installed. options String or Array of Strings none Extra flags for the install or remove command, placed before the package name. A String is used as is; Array elements are each shell-quoted. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

docs.title: Commands per package manager
docs.text:
NAME is the package name, OPTIONS the options: value.

Manager Detected on Installed when Install Remove apt ID or ID_LIKE is debian, ubuntu dpkg-query -W -f='${Status}' NAME ends in installed DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y OPTIONS NAME DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get remove -y OPTIONS NAME dnf rhel, centos, fedora, rocky, almalinux, ol rpm -q NAME exits 0 dnf install -y OPTIONS NAME dnf remove -y OPTIONS NAME apk alpine apk info -e NAME exits 0 apk add OPTIONS NAME apk del OPTIONS NAME pacman arch, archarm, manjaro, endeavouros pacman -Q NAME exits 0 pacman -S --needed --noconfirm OPTIONS NAME pacman -Rns --noconfirm OPTIONS NAME

Index refreshes:

  • apt: DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get update runs once per apply, right before the first install. Runs that install nothing never touch the network.
  • dnf and apk refresh their metadata themselves.
  • pacman: sadame never runs pacman -Sy. Refreshing the sync database without upgrading (-Sy without -u) is a partial upgrade, which Arch does not support. Keep the system upgraded with pacman -Syu as usual.

docs.title: AUR packages
docs.text:
The package resource does not install from the AUR in this release. Until it does, use an AUR helper such as yay or paru through exec, guarded so it only runs when the package is missing:

examples/resources/package/aur.rb
# AUR packages are not handled by the package resource in sadame 0.1. Use an
# AUR helper through exec, guarded so it only runs when the package is
# missing and the helper is installed. yay and paru refuse to run as root,
# so the command runs as the user named in vars[:aur_user].
exec "runuser -u #{vars[:aur_user]} -- yay -S --needed --noconfirm visual-studio-code-bin",
     only_if: "command -v yay",
     not_if: "pacman -Q visual-studio-code-bin"
examples/resources/package/vars.rb
# The AUR helper must run as a normal user. When sadame runs through sudo,
# SUDO_USER is the user who called it.
{
  aur_user: ENV["SUDO_USER"] || ENV["USER"]
}

AUR helpers refuse to run as root, which is why the command goes through runuser. The helper then calls sudo pacman itself, so that user needs to be able to run pacman with sudo without a password prompt: sadame runs commands with standard input closed and cannot answer one. Without yay installed, only_if skips the resource:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/package/aur.rb
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Arch Linux)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Fresh Arch containers have no sync database. In the archlinux Docker image, pacman -S warns "database file for 'core' does not exist" and fails with "target not found" until pacman -Syu has run once. Installed systems do not have this problem.
  • Package groups and virtual packages. The installed check asks for the exact name. A group such as base-devel on Arch, or a name that is only provided by another package, never reports as installed, so it shows up in every plan. Declare the member packages instead.
  • Expecting upgrades. state: :installed means "some version is installed". Sadame does not upgrade packages in this release.
  • Mixing families without a condition. package "apache2" on Rocky fails at apply time with the package manager's own error.

docs.text:

docs.title: service
docs.text: service manages a systemd unit: whether it starts at boot (enable) and whether it is running now (state). It reads the current state with systemctl is-enabled and systemctl is-active and only calls systemctl to change what differs. Other resources can ask a service to reload or restart when they change, through notifies:.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/service/recipe.rb
# On Arch, installing nginx does not enable or start it; the service
# resource does. Debian and Ubuntu start services on install, so there the
# same resource usually reports no change.
package "nginx"
service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description enable true or false unmanaged Start at boot (systemctl enable) or not (systemctl disable). Enabled means systemctl is-enabled prints enabled. state :running or :stopped unmanaged Running now (systemctl start) or not (systemctl stop). Running means systemctl is-active prints active. user String none Manage the unit in this user's systemd instance (systemctl --user -M USER@), such as a unit in ~/.config/systemd/user/. The user must be logged in or have lingering enabled (loginctl enable-linger USER). notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

A service with neither option manages nothing by itself; it is still a valid target for notifications.

docs.title: Actions for notifications
docs.text:
Other resources can trigger these with notifies: [:action, "service[name]"]:

Action Runs :start systemctl start NAME :stop systemctl stop NAME :restart systemctl restart NAME :reload systemctl reload NAME :enable systemctl enable NAME :disable systemctl disable NAME

Actions run only when the notifying resource changed. By default they run once each, after all resources; add :immediately to run one right away. See the scenario below and Notifications.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/service/recipe.rb
# On Arch, installing nginx does not enable or start it; the service
# resource does. Debian and Ubuntu start services on install, so there the
# same resource usually reports no change.

docs.title: Reloading after a configuration change
docs.text:
examples/resources/service/reload_on_change.rb
# Reload nginx when its configuration changes. The reload runs once, at the
# end of apply, and only if the file changed.
package "nginx"

file "/etc/nginx/conf.d/status.conf",
     content: "server {\n  listen 127.0.0.1:8080;\n  location = /status { stub_status; }\n}\n",
     mode: "0644",
     notifies: [:reload, "service[nginx]"]

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No systemd. The resource needs a running systemd (it checks for /run/systemd/system). In containers without systemd, and on Alpine with OpenRC, it fails with "systemd is not running on this host".
  • Declaring the service before its package. On a fresh machine the unit does not exist yet, so plan shows it as disabled and stopped, and apply fails if the package comes later in the recipe. Put package first.
  • Units that cannot be enabled. systemctl is-enabled prints static for units without an [Install] section. Those never count as enabled, so enable: true on them shows a change on every plan. Leave enable out.
  • Expecting a reload when only the service changed. reload and restart happen only through notifications from other resources.
  • Reloading a service that cannot reload. systemctl reload fails for units without ExecReload=. Notify :restart for those.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• package to install the software first.
  • file for configuration files that notify the service.

docs.title: user
docs.text: user manages a local Linux user account: whether it exists, its UID, home directory, login shell, and the groups it must belong to. It reads the account with getent passwd and id -nG, and changes it with useradd, usermod and userdel only when something differs.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/user/minimal.rb
user "deploy"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description uid Integer unmanaged Numeric user ID. home String unmanaged Home directory path. shell String unmanaged Login shell, such as "/bin/bash" or "/usr/sbin/nologin". groups Array of Strings unmanaged Groups the user must belong to. Other memberships are left alone. The groups must exist. system true or false false Create a system account (useradd -r), which gets no home directory. Only used when the user is created. state :present or :absent :present :absent deletes the account with userdel; the home directory is kept. notifies [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on other resources when this one changes. See Notifications. subscribes [:action, "type[name]"], optionally with :immediately, or a list of them none Actions to run on this resource when another one changes.

New users that are not system users get a home directory (useradd -m). Changing home on an existing user updates the account but does not move files.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/user/recipe.rb
# A login user who belongs to at least the adm group.
user "deploy", shell: "/bin/bash", groups: ["adm"]

# A system user without a login shell.
user "svc-backup", system: true, home: "/var/lib/svc-backup", shell: "/usr/sbin/nologin"

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Groups that do not exist yet. useradd -G docker fails if the docker group has not been created. Declare the package that creates it first.
  • Alpine without shadow. Alpine's BusyBox has no useradd. Declare package "shadow" before any user resource; without it the resource fails with a message saying so.
  • Expecting a group list to be exact. Removing a group from groups: does not remove the user from that group.
  • Clashing with existing accounts. Many distributions ship system users such as backup or www-data. Declaring one of those with a different home or shell changes the existing account.
